items.title: ABBACARE: How Kano is expanding healthcare access for the most vulnerable
items.description: By Hassan A. Karofi Access to affordable healthcare remains a major challenge for millions of Nigerians, particularly low-income households and vulnerable groups who often delay or forgo treatment because of the cost. In Kano State, the ABBACARE Initiative is one of the interventions aimed at addressing this challenge through social health insurance. Implemented by the Kano State Contributory Healthcare Management Agency (KSCHMA), ABBACARE is designed to provide healthcare coverage for vulnerable groups, including pregnant women, persons living with sickle cell disorder and emergency patients. Its focus is on reducing the financial barriers that prevent people from accessing essential medical services. According to figures provided for the initiative, ABBACARE has enrolled 28,721 beneficiaries and extended service delivery to 13 hospitals across Kano State’s three senatorial zones. These figures point to an effort to widen access to healthcare, although the programme’s long-term impact will depend on the quality of services available, the regularity of funding and the ability to sustain coverage as more people are enrolled. The initiative also highlights the role state governments can play in advancing Universal Health Coverage through social health insurance. While national policies provide an important framework, state-level programmes such as ABBACARE can help address local healthcare needs and extend financial protection to people who might otherwise struggle to pay for treatment. The programme is part of a wider set of health interventions under Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf’s administration. Another is the Gida-Gida Lafiya Project, which focuses on hypertension and other non-communicable diseases through the distribution of customised digital blood pressure monitors. The devices are intended to help beneficiaries monitor their blood pressure, identify possible health risks early and seek medical attention when necessary. Their adaptation to provide guidance in local languages also reflects the importance of making health information accessible to people in their communities. Although ABBACARE and Gida-Gida Lafiya address different aspects of healthcare, they speak to two related challenges. The former seeks to reduce the financial burden of accessing treatment, while the latter encourages prevention, regular monitoring and early intervention. Both approaches are relevant in a health system where the cost of treatment and late presentation at hospitals can worsen health outcomes. However, the success of such interventions should not be measured by enrolment figures or the number of devices distributed alone. Their value will ultimately depend on whether beneficiaries can consistently access the services promised, whether participating hospitals have the capacity to provide quality care and whether the programmes are adequately funded over time. The Kano State Ministry of Health and the leadership of KSCHMA therefore have important roles to play in ensuring that the initiatives deliver their intended benefits. Dr Rahila Mukhtar, whose role in the agency’s operations and healthcare financing efforts has been noteworthy, is among the key figures associated with the implementation of approaches such as ABBACARE. The agency’s work in administering the initiative underscores the importance of effective health insurance management. Enrolling vulnerable people is an important first step, but maintaining reliable access to care requires proper coordination with healthcare providers, transparent management of funds, regular monitoring and accountability to beneficiaries. For Kano, the next task is to consolidate the gains made through ABBACARE and ensure that the programme remains accessible and sustainable. Expanding coverage will also require attention to the capacity of participating hospitals and the experiences of beneficiaries, particularly those who depend on the scheme for maternal care, treatment of sickle cell disorder and emergency services. Other states can draw useful lessons from Kano’s experience, especially in using social health insurance to protect vulnerable populations. However, the model’s wider relevance will depend on evidence of its outcomes, affordability and sustainability. As Nigeria pursues Universal Health Coverage, initiatives such as ABBACARE show why state-level action matters. The real measure of progress will not simply be the number of people enrolled, but whether they can obtain timely, affordable and quality healthcare when they need it. •Karofi writes from Abuja and can be reached at hassankarofi@gmail.com. The post ABBACARE: How Kano is expanding healthcare access for the most vulnerable appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: ASIWAJU: Why I support 2nd term for President Tinubu
items.description: By Moriamoh Ojikutu A friend asked me recently, “Do you think Asiwaju is working?” My answer was simple: “Yes. He is doing his job.” Let me be clear about where I stand. I strongly support President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and his administration, and I want him re-elected for a second term. I believe in his leadership and the direction of his administration. I want him to complete the work he has started and deliver the lasting improvements I believe are possible. That does not mean I think everything is perfect. It certainly does not mean I am unaware of the difficulties Nigerians are facing. I live here. I run businesses here. I employ people, pay bills, buy fuel and deal with rising costs. I know what it means to reconsider spending, adjust plans and keep going when doing business becomes more difficult. My support exists alongside that reality, not outside it. When I say he is doing his job, I mean that I believe he is confronting difficult problems rather than leaving them for someone else. But taking difficult decisions is not the finish line. Delivering results that Nigerians can see, touch and feel is. Reform Is Rarely Comfortable: I do not believe Nigeria’s economic difficulties began with this administration, nor do I believe every problem can be resolved within a few years. My view is that some difficult decisions had been postponed for too long. President Tinubu’s administration has pursued major changes, including the removal of petrol subsidies and reforms to the foreign exchange system. I support the decision to confront those structural problems. But I also recognise the hardship Nigerians have experienced during this period. Families are making difficult choices. Businesses are adjusting their operations. People are working hard and still worrying about what they can afford. Those experiences deserve to be heard, not dismissed with political slogans. For me, acknowledging the pain does not mean rejecting the need for reform. It means asking how reform can be implemented more effectively and how people can be better protected through the transition. A policy can have a sound objective and still need adjustments. I want the government to listen, respond and improve what needs to work better. That is part of making reform succeed. We Should Acknowledge Meaningful Interventions: Alongside discussing the hardship, I believe we should recognise interventions intended to help people. NELFUND provides interest-free loans to help eligible students overcome financial barriers to higher education, with support for institutional fees and/or upkeep. These are loans with repayment obligations, not grants. For a student facing the possibility of leaving school because of money, access to financial support can make a meaningful difference. Education is one of the areas in which I want government intervention to open doors. MAMII is another initiative I welcome. It focuses on reducing maternal and newborn deaths through measures that include improving access to care, strengthening referral systems and helping services respond to complications during pregnancy and childbirth. As a country, we should care deeply about whether mothers can access care and whether students can continue their education. These programmes deserve attention, alongside honest questions about whom they are reaching, how effectively they are operating and what results they are delivering. I want them strengthened and delivered well. Recognising their value does not mean declaring the work complete. It means making room for a fair assessment of the administration. Accountability at Every Level: I expect leadership from the president. I also expect governors, local government chairmen, legislators and ministers to fulfil their responsibilities. Holding the presidency accountable should be the beginning of a wider demand for good governance, not the end of it. When communities lack functioning schools, healthcare, drainage or clean water, citizens should ask which institutions are responsible, what resources they have received and what they have delivered. We should ask these questions consistently, regardless of party affiliation. What is happening in our states? What is happening in our local governments? What are the people representing us doing with the responsibilities entrusted to them? I want this presidency to succeed, and I want every other level of government to do its part. Nigeria needs more than one office working. It needs public institutions and officials taking their responsibilities seriously. Public Money Must Deliver Public Value: Government must be able to explain what citizens’ sacrifices are achieving. Where revenues and allocations increase, people deserve to know how those resources are being used. How much was received? What was budgeted? What was spent? What was completed? And how has it improved people’s lives? These should be normal questions, not uncomfortable ones. I want to see public money translate into better schools, accessible healthcare, reliable infrastructure and essential services. I want clear reporting that allows citizens to judge performance beyond speeches and announcements. Public funds are not personal gifts from politicians. They are resources held in trust for the people. That trust must be respected at every level of government. Security Must Remain a Priority: Security is central to the Nigeria I want to see. Our farmers should be able to work without fear. Families should be able to travel safely. Communities should be protected, and businesses should be able to operate with confidence. These are not partisan expectations. They are basic expectations of government. I want the administration’s economic ambitions to be matched by sustained improvements in security. Progress must be felt in people’s confidence that they can travel, earn a living and go about their daily lives safely. That is an essential part of the success I want for this presidency. Support Should Not Require Blindness: I sometimes find our political culture exhausting. Apparently, you must either support everything a government does or oppose everything it does. There seems to be little room for thoughtful disagreement. I reject that thinking. I can support President Tinubu and question how a policy is being implemented. I can acknowledge progress and ask for greater urgency elsewhere. I can support the APC and still expect its public officials to explain their decisions and account for public resources. There is no contradiction in that. My questions do not come from uncertainty about where I stand. They come from wanting an administration I support to succeed. Loyalty should not mean silence. Criticism should not automatically mean opposition. We need room for honest conversations about what is working, what is not and what must happen next. That is the kind of political participation I believe in: committed, constructive and willing to speak honestly. Why I Support a Second Term: I want President Tinubu re-elected for a second term because I believe in his leadership and want him to complete the work he has begun. I believe continuity offers an opportunity to build on these reforms, improve their implementation and turn policy changes into improvements people can feel. That is my conviction, not a belief that time alone will solve our problems. Nigerians need relief today. People need affordable food, access to healthcare, reliable electricity, security and opportunities for their children. They need an economy in which hard work offers a reasonable chance of a decent living. Those expectations are fair, and I want this administration to meet them with greater urgency. For me, a second term should be an opportunity to build on what is working, correct what is not and deliver more widely. I want stronger businesses, functioning institutions, better infrastructure and genuine opportunities for young Nigerians. I want the sacrifices of this period to lead somewhere meaningful. And I want a government that understands that the patience of the people must never be taken for granted. Hope, With Its Eyes Open: So, why Asiwaju? Because I believe in President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s leadership, I support his administration, and I want him re-elected for a second term. I want him to complete the work he has started and turn the promise of these reforms into lasting improvements in the lives of Nigerians. I do not dismiss the hardship people are facing, and my support does not mean silence when something needs to improve. I want this presidency to succeed and I want that success to be felt in our homes, our businesses and our communities. That is where I stand: firmly in support, clear about my expectations, and hopeful for Nigeria. Hope, with its eyes open. The post ASIWAJU: Why I support 2nd term for President Tinubu appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Why construction could become Africa’s key technology, investment opportunity
items.description: By Jimoh Razaq For years, Africa’s technology ecosystem has concentrated much of its entrepreneurial energy, investment capital and innovation around fintech, e-commerce, mobility, telecommunications and entertainment. These sectors have produced remarkable companies, attracted international investment and demonstrated that African businesses can build technology products capable of scaling across borders. But there is another industry with enormous economic significance, deeply entrenched inefficiencies and a largely untapped opportunity for technological transformation: construction. It is an industry that builds our homes, roads, hospitals, schools, factories, power infrastructure and cities. It employs millions of people, supports extensive manufacturing and distribution networks, moves significant volumes of capital and sits at the centre of economic development. Yet much of its operational infrastructure remains fragmented, manual and inefficient. While technology has transformed how people transfer money, order food, book transportation and access entertainment, the processes through which buildings and infrastructure are planned, financed, procured and delivered remain remarkably difficult to coordinate. This is not simply an operational inconvenience. It is a massive economic opportunity. The next generation of transformative African technology companies may emerge from solving the problems of the industries that physically build Africa. The industry technology has overlooked Construction is one of the world’s largest economic sectors. Global construction output was approximately $13 trillion in 2023, with projections suggesting it could reach $22 trillion by 2040. Yet its productivity performance remains disappointing. McKinsey’s 2024 research found that global construction productivity grew by approximately 0.4 per cent annually between 2000 and 2022, compared with around 2 per cent for the broader economy. This represents a productivity improvement of only about 10 per cent over more than two decades. The implications are significant. Projects experience delays. Budgets become unreliable. Material procurement remains fragmented. Labour productivity is difficult to measure. Project information is scattered across emails, spreadsheets, paper documents and messaging applications. Developers, contractors, consultants, suppliers, artisans and investors often operate without a shared information environment. These challenges are particularly visible in emerging markets, where informal transactions, inconsistent data, financing constraints and infrastructure limitations compound existing industry inefficiencies. Africa’s infrastructure ambitions make the opportunity even more important. The OECD’s Africa’s Development Dynamics 2025 estimates that investing approximately $155 billion annually in infrastructure could significantly accelerate the continent’s economic growth. The question is not whether Africa needs more construction. It clearly does. The question is whether the industry can deliver the volume of housing, infrastructure and commercial development required without fundamentally changing how it operates. That is where technology founders should pay attention. Construction is not just an engineering industry. It is a technology ecosystem waiting to be connected. One of the biggest misconceptions about construction technology is that innovation is primarily about drones, robotics, 3D printing or sophisticated building design software. Those technologies matter, but they represent only a fraction of the opportunity. Construction is also an industry of financial transactions, procurement networks, logistics, labour coordination, data management, risk assessment, asset management and complex workflows. Every construction project creates multiple interconnected problems that technology can solve. Consider what happens when someone decides to build a house. They need to verify land ownership, develop architectural and structural drawings, estimate project costs, secure financing, identify qualified professionals, procure materials, engage artisans, manage construction activities, monitor expenditure and verify completion. Each stage involves multiple stakeholders, financial commitments and operational decisions. In many African markets, these activities are still managed through disconnected systems. There is an opportunity to build technology infrastructure that connects this entire process. Opportunities that could redefine construction in Africa AI-powered construction cost intelligence: One of the most persistent problems in construction is inaccurate project costing. Material prices fluctuate. Labour rates differ by location. Transportation costs change. Exchange-rate movements affect imported materials, while poor historical data makes reliable forecasting difficult. An intelligent construction cost engine could combine material prices, labour rates, geographical information, historical project costs and market conditions to generate more reliable estimates. Imagine a developer being able to estimate the cost of constructing a residential building in Lagos, Abuja, Ibadan or Accra using current market information rather than relying entirely on outdated rate books. This is an opportunity for AI engineers, data scientists and construction professionals to build genuinely useful products. Digital construction material marketplaces: The procurement of cement, reinforcement steel, roofing materials, electrical fittings, plumbing components and other construction products remains highly fragmented. Buyers frequently depend on personal contacts, multiple quotations and informal supplier relationships. A verified digital marketplace could connect manufacturers, distributors, suppliers, contractors and developers through transparent pricing, product verification, digital payments and delivery tracking. Beyond convenience, such a platform could improve price discovery, reduce procurement fraud and create a more accountable supply chain. Save-To-Build financial technology: Millions of people want to build houses but cannot finance the entire project at once. Traditional construction financing is often inaccessible, while informal savings arrangements do not necessarily provide the structure or safeguards required for long-term building projects. A Save-To-Build platform could allow individuals to accumulate funds towards clearly defined construction milestones. For example, a customer could save towards land documentation, architectural design, foundation construction, roofing and finishing. Funds could be released against verified milestones, supported by appropriate financial safeguards and partnerships with regulated financial institutions. This creates an opportunity to connect personal finance, construction delivery and financial inclusion. AI-powered site supervision and project intelligence: Construction sites generate enormous amounts of information, but much of it is not systematically captured or analysed. Artificial intelligence, computer vision and mobile technology could help monitor construction progress, identify deviations from approved designs, track material consumption, record labour attendance and flag potential safety issues. A project owner could receive a digital site performance report without having to depend exclusively on periodic manual updates. The goal is not to replace professional site supervision or engineering judgement. It is to equip professionals with better information to make faster and more informed decisions. 5. Skilled labour and artisan marketplaces Africa’s construction industry depends heavily on skilled and semi-skilled workers, many of whom operate within informal employment networks. Finding reliable masons, electricians, plumbers, tilers, welders, carpenters and other artisans can be difficult. A structured digital marketplace could provide verified profiles, skills assessments, ratings, work histories, location-based discovery and protected payment arrangements. Such platforms could also create opportunities for professional training, certification and workforce development. Technology can help formalise an important part of the construction economy without excluding the people who already work within it. Digital property development and off-plan sales platforms: Property developers frequently sell units before construction is completed. However, buyers may struggle to obtain reliable information about construction progress, payment schedules, contractual obligations and project delivery. A digital off-plan platform could provide verified developer profiles, interactive property models, payment tracking, digital contracts and construction progress updates. This would improve transparency and help restore confidence in property development markets. Modular and industrialised construction technology: Construction technology should not be limited to software. There is a significant opportunity in developing prefabricated building systems, modular housing components, standardised structural elements and rapid-assembly construction solutions. Combining digital design, manufacturing automation and efficient project logistics could reduce construction time, material waste and repetitive site activities. This is particularly relevant to affordable housing, student accommodation, healthcare facilities and standardised institutional buildings. Construction logistics and material tracking: Materials and equipment move continuously between manufacturers, warehouses, suppliers, transport operators and construction sites. Poor coordination leads to delayed deliveries, unnecessary transportation costs, material losses and idle equipment. Internet of Things technology, QR codes, GPS tracking and logistics management software could provide greater visibility across the supply chain. Developers could know what has been ordered, what has been dispatched, what has arrived and what has actually been consumed on site. Digital building approvals and regulatory platforms: Building approval processes can involve several agencies, professional submissions, inspections and compliance requirements. Technology could help digitise application processing, document verification, inspection scheduling, permit tracking and regulatory records. A properly integrated platform would improve transparency, reduce administrative delays and make compliance easier to monitor. Governments could also benefit from better urban development data and more efficient building control. AI-powered construction education and workforce development: Africa cannot build the infrastructure it needs without a skilled construction workforce. There is an opportunity to develop digital learning platforms for artisans, technicians, junior engineers, quantity surveyors, project managers and other construction professionals. Artificial intelligence could personalise learning, provide technical explanations in accessible language and support practical training. Local language support, including Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo and Pidgin, could make technical education more accessible to workers who may not benefit from conventional English-language training alone. Land intelligence and title verification: Land ownership and title verification remain significant challenges in many African property markets. Technology platforms could integrate land registry records, survey information, ownership documentation, encumbrance checks and geographic information systems. Where government data access and legal frameworks permit, secure verification APIs could help professionals, developers, investors and financial institutions conduct more reliable due diligence. This could reduce information asymmetry and improve confidence in property transactions. Digital estate and infrastructure planning: Housing developments require more than individual buildings. They require roads, drainage, electricity, water supply, waste management and other essential infrastructure. Digital planning tools could integrate land surveys, topographical data, engineering designs, utility networks and development requirements to support more efficient estate planning. AI-assisted design could help professionals evaluate alternative layouts, estimate infrastructure costs and identify potential planning constraints. Integrated construction collaboration platforms: Perhaps one of the most important opportunities is the creation of a shared digital workspace for the entire construction value chain. Architects, engineers, quantity surveyors, contractors, developers, suppliers and clients need to work with the same project information. A centralised collaboration platform could connect drawings, revisions, bills of quantities, procurement, contracts, schedules, budgets, site reports, payments and project performance. Think of it as the digital operating system for a construction project. Rather than managing every activity through disconnected applications, stakeholders could operate within a coordinated environment. Why this opportunity is bigger than another startup trend There is a temptation to approach construction technology as another opportunity to build an application, raise venture capital and pursue rapid user acquisition. That would be a mistake. Construction technology requires a deeper understanding of the industry. A product that works in a conventional consumer technology environment may fail on a construction site if it does not account for procurement practices, professional responsibilities, contractual relationships, payment structures, regulatory requirements and the realities of field operations. The most successful founders will not necessarily be those who write the best code. They will be those who understand the problems deeply enough to build technology that people are willing to use repeatedly. This requires collaboration between technology founders and construction professionals. Software engineers need to understand construction workflows. Construction professionals need to become more comfortable with data, automation and digital systems. Investors need to understand that some construction technology products require longer adoption cycles but can eventually become deeply embedded in the industry. There is also a need to build for Africa’s realities rather than simply importing solutions designed for different markets. Products must account for fragmented supply chains, mobile-first users, varying levels of digital literacy, unreliable connectivity in some locations, local payment systems, regulatory differences and the informal economy. Technology must simplify the industry, not make it more complicated. The investment opportunity: from individual applications to industry infrastructure The most interesting opportunities may not necessarily be standalone applications. They may be the platforms that become essential infrastructure for how the industry operates. A material marketplace that becomes the primary procurement channel for thousands of contractors. A financial technology platform that manages construction savings, project financing and milestone payments. A project management system that becomes the standard operating environment for developers and contractors. A labour marketplace that connects millions of skilled workers with verified opportunities. An AI-powered construction intelligence platform that becomes an essential tool for estimating, planning and monitoring projects. Each of these businesses could develop substantial commercial value if it achieves product-market fit, trusted distribution and sustainable unit economics. They also create opportunities for interconnected ecosystems. For example, a construction cost platform can connect to a material marketplace. The marketplace can connect to financing. Financing can connect to project monitoring. Project monitoring can connect to procurement and payment verification. This is how technology can move beyond isolated applications and become an operating layer for an entire industry. The role of governments and institutional investors The transformation of construction cannot be left to startups alone. Governments control important parts of the enabling environment, including land administration, building regulations, public procurement, infrastructure investment and access to official records. They should create opportunities for responsible technology companies to participate in digitising these systems. Public agencies can support interoperable data standards, transparent procurement processes, digital building approval systems and reliable property information infrastructure. Financial institutions and institutional investors also have a role to play. Construction technology companies may require patient capital, industry partnerships and access to real project environments to validate their solutions. Venture capital firms should look beyond the familiar consumer technology categories and examine businesses that improve productivity across construction, infrastructure and industrial supply chains. The OECD’s infrastructure investment analysis makes clear that Africa’s development ambitions require substantial capital mobilisation. Technology will be essential in improving how that capital is translated into productive assets. Africa needs builders who understand both code and concrete I believe we are approaching an important moment in the evolution of African technology. The continent has demonstrated that it can develop financial technology platforms, digital marketplaces and innovative consumer products. The next opportunity is to apply that same entrepreneurial energy to the industries that underpin economic development. Construction is one of them. The opportunity is not simply to digitise paperwork or replace manual processes with mobile applications. It is to redesign how projects are financed, planned, procured, executed and managed. It is to make construction more transparent, more productive, more predictable and more accessible. It is to use technology to reduce waste, improve project delivery, expand access to housing and accelerate infrastructure development. This is also the thinking behind what we are developing with Ladaar: a connected construction technology ecosystem bringing together construction finance, professional services, procurement, project intelligence and workflow automation. But the opportunity extends far beyond one company or one platform. Africa needs many more innovators willing to understand this industry and build solutions around its real problems. The next generation of technology leaders should look beyond the sectors that have already attracted the most attention. They should look at the industries where inefficiencies are deepest, where the economic stakes are highest and where technology can produce tangible improvements in people’s lives. Africa does not just need more technology companies. It needs technology companies that can help build Africa. The next great African technology opportunity may not be another application for transferring money, ordering food or booking a ride. It may be the technology that helps us build a million homes, deliver infrastructure more efficiently, connect construction professionals, finance projects responsibly and create better cities. The future of African technology will not be written by code alone. It will also be built with concrete, steel, data and innovation. And it is time the technology ecosystem paid attention. Razaq is a construction and project management professional The post Why construction could become Africa’s key technology, investment opportunity appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: The future of automobile technology: Embracing AI for business growth in Nigeria
items.description: By Moses Stowe The growing importance of technological innovation, professional development and sustainable business growth in Nigeria’s automobile industry took centre stage at the 2026 Nigeria Automobile Technicians Association (NATA), Lagos State Council Day, where Intercontinental Distillers Limited (IDL), makers of Action Bitters, participated in an initiative recognising and supporting the contributions of automobile technicians to the nation’s economy. Held under the theme, “Harnessing Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Transform and Develop the Business of Auto Technicians in Nigeria,” this year’s celebration provided an important platform for industry stakeholders, automobile professionals, corporate organisations and association leaders to examine emerging opportunities in the automotive sector and the need to equip technicians with the knowledge, skills and resources required to remain competitive in an increasingly technology-driven industry. A major highlight of IDL’s participation was its support for the empowerment of automobile technicians through the provision of automobile tools. The initiative underscored the importance of practical support in strengthening the capacity of technicians, improving their operational efficiency and helping them deliver better services to customers. Beyond the recognition of their professional contributions, the gesture reflected the importance of providing tangible resources that can support the growth and sustainability of small businesses within the automobile value chain. Speaking on the significance of the occasion, Celestine Anyanwu, Brand Manager, Wine and Bitters, IDL, acknowledged the invaluable contributions of automobile technicians to the nation’s economic and industrial development. He noted that their expertise, dedication and entrepreneurial spirit remain essential to the effective functioning of the transportation and automobile sectors. He emphasised the importance of initiatives that recognise the efforts of professionals whose daily activities contribute to keeping businesses, individuals and transportation systems running. According to him, supporting the NATA community through the provision of relevant automobile tools represents a meaningful contribution towards professional development, business improvement and the advancement of the automobile servicing industry. He further acknowledged the relevance of this year’s theme, noting that Artificial Intelligence presents emerging opportunities for automobile technicians to improve diagnostic processes, embrace modern automotive technologies and develop more efficient approaches to business operations. He encouraged industry stakeholders to continue supporting platforms that promote innovation, practical empowerment and sustainable professional growth. One of the major highlights of the event was the presentation of the grand prize, a complete set of automobile tool kits, to Kazeem Oladeji, one of the beneficiaries of the empowerment initiative. Expressing his appreciation, Oladeji described the award as a significant boost to his profession and business, noting that access to the right tools is essential to delivering quality automobile services. He commended Action Bitters and Intercontinental Distillers Limited for recognising the efforts of automobile technicians and extending support beyond mere celebration to practical empowerment. In the address of the Chairman of NATA, Lagos State Council, Morufu Egberongbe, described the celebration as a significant milestone in the association’s collective journey towards the growth, recognition, empowerment and professional development of automobile technicians across Lagos State and Nigeria. He reaffirmed the association’s commitment to promoting professionalism, unity, excellence and sustainable business development among its members, who operate across different segments of the automotive value chain. These include auto mechanics, auto electricians, panel beaters, spray painters, vulcanisers, auto air-conditioning technicians, diagnostic specialists, spare parts dealers and other related professionals. Egberongbe explained that the choice of this year’s theme reflected NATA’s determination to embrace innovation and adequately prepare its members for the future of the automotive industry. He noted that Artificial Intelligence and other emerging technologies are creating new possibilities for vehicle diagnostics, maintenance, customer service and business management, making continuous learning and adaptation increasingly important. The NATA chairman also expressed appreciation to corporate partners, sponsors and exhibitors for recognising the importance of the automobile technician community and supporting initiatives that promote innovation, capacity development and business growth. He described their contributions as investments in the future of the automotive industry and the thousands of businesses sustained by the sector. He equally acknowledged government institutions, industry leaders, association executives, the planning committee and other stakeholders whose contributions helped make the celebration a success. For IDL, its participation in the 2026 NATA Lagos State Council Day provided an opportunity to recognise a professional community whose contributions extend beyond automobile repairs to entrepreneurship, employment generation, technical expertise and economic development. The provision of automobile tools also highlighted an important dimension of corporate engagement: the need to support professional communities with resources that address practical business needs. For automobile technicians, access to appropriate tools is essential to improving service delivery, adapting to changing vehicle technologies and maintaining the confidence of customers. As Nigeria’s automotive landscape continues to evolve, the integration of Artificial Intelligence, digital diagnostic systems and modern vehicle maintenance solutions will increasingly shape the industry’s future. Platforms such as the NATA Lagos State Council Day therefore remain important in encouraging collaboration, knowledge exchange and stronger partnerships between professional associations and corporate stakeholders. Ultimately, the 2026 celebration reinforced a shared vision of an automobile industry built on technical competence, innovation, professional recognition and economic empowerment. Through its participation and support for the initiative, IDL joined other stakeholders in recognising the importance of strengthening the capabilities of automobile technicians and creating opportunities for the continued development of their businesses. The message was clear: the future of Nigeria’s automobile industry depends not only on technological advancement but also on empowering the skilled professionals who make the sector work. The post The future of automobile technology: Embracing AI for business growth in Nigeria appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Oando’s rising fortunes: How Wale Tinubu is rewriting growth story
items.description: By Adebayo Adeoye Jubril Adewale Tinubu, CON, is not one to be easily satisfied with yesterday’s accomplishments. For the Oando Group Chief Executive, every milestone appears to present another opportunity to raise the bar, test new possibilities and push the boundaries of what an indigenous energy company can achieve. That restless ambition is once again finding expression in Oando’s improving fortunes. At Oando, the story has never been one of an overnight success. Rather, it is a tale of calculated risks, corporate reinvention and an unwavering belief in the possibilities of indigenous enterprise. Over the years, Tinubu has remained at the centre of the company’s evolution, steering its affairs through difficult economic seasons, industry uncertainties and the complex demands of a rapidly changing energy landscape. Today, the signs of another promising chapter are becoming increasingly visible, as the indigenous energy company continues to record encouraging improvements in its operations, strengthening its position in an industry where survival and relevance are often determined by the ability to anticipate change and respond decisively. For Tinubu, who has spent considerable years building Oando into a recognisable name in Africa’s energy industry, the latest developments represent more than a corporate milestone. They reflect an enduring ambition to build an indigenous institution capable of competing beyond Nigeria’s shores and holding its own among established players in the global energy market. One of the most encouraging aspects of Oando’s recent performance is the improvement in its operational efficiency. The company has continued to strengthen its production capacity, improve asset utilisation and address some of the operational challenges that have historically confronted the oil and gas industry. Its improving production profile suggests that the investments and management decisions taken over time are beginning to yield meaningful results. But beyond increased production, the company’s efforts to reduce operating costs and improve facility reliability have equally attracted attention. In an industry where operational disruptions can quickly erode profitability, efficiency remains a critical ingredient for sustainable growth. Oando’s renewed focus on operational discipline therefore speaks to a management philosophy that recognises the importance of building a business on solid foundations rather than merely pursuing expansion for its own sake. Indeed, Tinubu’s corporate journey has been defined by an appetite for ambitious decisions. His leadership at Oando has seen the company navigate major transitions, expand its interests and deepen its participation in Nigeria’s energy value chain. The acquisition of additional upstream assets further underscored his belief that indigenous companies should not remain spectators in an industry that has for decades been dominated by international oil companies. That ambition, however, comes with its own demands. The acquisition and development of oil and gas assets require substantial capital, careful financial management and the ability to balance immediate obligations with long-term business objectives. Oando is not insulated from these pressures, particularly as it continues to manage the financial commitments associated with its expansion strategy. Nevertheless, the company’s improving operating performance offers reasons for optimism. Its ability to generate cash from operations while maintaining investments in drilling and other production-related activities demonstrates a determination to sustain its growth trajectory. Equally important is the company’s continuing effort to strengthen its financial position and manage its borrowing obligations. For Tinubu, the task is clearly not simply to preserve what has already been built but to ensure that Oando remains relevant in an industry undergoing profound transformation. The global conversation around energy security, cleaner energy sources and sustainable development is changing the rules of engagement. Indigenous energy companies must therefore demonstrate not only financial resilience but also the capacity to adapt to emerging realities. This is where the Oando story becomes particularly interesting. Tinubu has consistently projected the ambition of an African entrepreneur who believes that local businesses can rise above structural limitations and compete on a much bigger stage. His approach has been characterised by bold corporate moves, strategic partnerships and an understanding that the future belongs to companies willing to evolve. Yet, beyond the boardroom calculations and corporate announcements, there is also the question of legacy. Building a successful company is one thing; establishing an institution that can withstand changing leadership, economic cycles and industry disruptions is another. It is a challenge that every ambitious business leader must eventually confront. For now, Oando appears determined to keep its place in the unfolding energy narrative. Its improving operational fortunes provide fresh momentum, while Tinubu’s leadership continues to attract attention as the company pursues its broader ambitions. Clearly, the Oando story is far from finished. And if the current momentum is anything to go by, Wale Tinubu is not ready to take his foot off the accelerator. In the competitive race for relevance in Africa’s energy industry, he appears determined to ensure that Oando is not merely present at the table but has a voice in deciding where the industry goes. Adeoye Adebayo writes in from Lagos. The post Oando’s rising fortunes: How Wale Tinubu is rewriting growth story appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 2027: Imperative of Peter Mbah’s second term in Enugu
items.description: By Willy Eya Politics apart, Enugu State Governor, Dr Peter Mbah deserves a second term in office. That is not contestable. Certainly, the governor’s achievements since assumption of office in 2023 will campaign for him ahead of the 2027 general elections. One good turn, they say, deserves another. Mbah came in as an accomplished technocrat determined to reshape the public sector using his private sector background.He approaches governance with a structured blueprint rather than the usual, impromptu trial-and-error tactics by regular Nigerian politicians. Every step the governor takes is intentional, hence, he links infrastructure directly to economic growth. His idea for instance is that fixing roads or investing heavily in security isn’t just for safety but a targeted prerequisite to open up the state for tourism, agriculture, and private sector investments. He deliberately avoided slow, conventional governance steps and pushed instead for immediate macro-level structural adjustments from Day One.Mbah’s strength lies in translating private-sector efficiency into public-sector execution.This quality is evidenced by his courage to dismantle slow legacy systems—such as implementing the fully digitized Enugu Geographic Information Service (ENGIS) to fast-track land administration and heavily relying on data to drive executive decisions. Unlike career politicians who rely on political patronage, the governor is largely a corporate technocrat whose leadership is rooted in rigorous planning. From inception after his inauguration, he was clear in his road-map to radically change the story of Enugu State. His first major challenge was to end the Monday Sit-at-Home disruptions. For years, the illegal “sit-at-home” orders crippled the economy of the Southeast and his immediate and uncompromising ban on the orders from his first week in office is frequently cited as a defining test of his leadership.Despite initial hiccups, the administration restored normal business and economic activities on Mondays and Enugu State is better for it today. In his cabinet appointments, Mbah consciously shifted the political culture of Enugu State by actively recruiting top-tier professionals from academia and the global private sector. He believes in inclusive and merit-based governance, hence, prioritized competence over partisan rewards. For him, governance is a serious business of service delivery, thus, he established a culture of accountability across state ministries. Knowing the importance of security to his set goals, he was quick to establish the Command and Control Centre which deployed modern surveillance and security infrastructure, including an ultramodern command and control center, to improve safety across the state. His administration has focused on a multi-faceted development framework aimed at growing the state’s economy from $4.4 billion to $30 billion. For many observers including this writer, that was a tall dream considering that hitherto, Enugu was largely a civil service state. He has proved pundits wrong as internal updates reveal a stark upward trajectory in the state’s fiscal performance, rising from ₦26 billion in 2022 to ₦181 billion in 2024, reaching ₦460 billion in 2025, and carrying an estimated projection of ₦871 billion for the 2026 fiscal year. So, the imperative of a second term for the governor, is strengthened by his administration’s documented performance, structural transformation and repositioning of the state since 2023. As the 2027 general elections approach, the voters would not forget the need to institutionalize ongoing economic reforms, finalize massive infrastructure projects, and sustain human capital developments that have redefined Enugu’s developmental trajectory. Across the state including the rural areas, there are visible projects and evidence of the administration’s commitment to improve public services. Governor Mbah’s ambitious vision to expand Enugu State’s economy from $4.4 billion to $30 billion and his obvious dogged determination to reposition Enugu State are his unique selling points. Part of the projects that would speak for Governor Mbah’s second term include 260 Smart Green Schools, 260 primary healthcare centres, an international hospital intended to reduce medical tourism and the establishment of Enugu Air which has already commenced international flights. The State’s fiscal architecture had undergone significant reform through revenue automation, reforms at the Enugu State Internal Revenue Service, improved financial management, the Treasury Single Account, enterprise resource planning and broader institutional restructuring. The administration has also ensured the sustenance of investments in youth empowerment, women development, technology, skills acquisition, social protection, tourism, environmental sustainability and community development. So,most critical observers agree that Enugu is on an aggressive path to development, and disrupting the upward momentum in 2027 would stall the state’s economic trajectory. It is then preposterous to imagine that people of the state will abandon Governor Mbah for a gamble with the opposition forces in next governorship election. Though opponents and paid social media activists point to economic hardships and taxes as issues in the coming election but objective and critical observers agree that the revolutionary reforms by the Enugu State government are laying a foundation for enduring progress and development of the state. It is not surprising that the governor’s supporters have moved away from the traditional political culture of treating a second term as an automatic entitlement but readily flaunt a data-backed scorecard to justify governance continuity. On September 6, 2026, Governor Mbah unveiled a compendium of more than 10,000 milestones recorded in the first term of his administration. Among others, the compendium records over 1,521 kilometres of constructed and reconstructed roads, over 7,000 classrooms, 260 Type-2 Primary Healthcare Centres, Enugu Air, the New Enugu Smart City, and the revamp of moribund assets. In an official manifesto performance review presented on October 29, 2026, Governor Mbah had noted that a second term is vital to deepen ongoing structural reforms and maximize completed projects rather than letting momentum stall. There is no doubt that re-electing him in the 2027 general elections would allow his administration to consolidate ongoing development projects, strengthen federal-state alignment, and expand economic opportunities. Willy is a member, Public Communication, Enugu State APC Campaign Council The post 2027: Imperative of Peter Mbah’s second term in Enugu appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Jospong subsidiary partners Turkish firm to test shrimp-shell-based farm products in Ghana
items.description: The African Agribusiness Consortium Limited (AAC), a subsidiary of the Jospong Group of Companies, has signed a memorandum of understanding with Türkiye-based ChitoGlobal Biotechnology to test agricultural products derived from discarded shrimp and crab shells on farms in Ghana. Signed on the sidelines of COP31 in Antalya, the agreement will begin with joint research and field trials to assess the products’ suitability for Ghanaian farming conditions. The products are based on chitosan, a substance derived from chitin, which is naturally found in the shells of crustaceans. The trials will examine whether the products can protect seeds and plants, improve crop resilience during dry spells and strengthen plants’ natural defences against fungal diseases. They will also assess the products’ effects on soil quality and crop yields, as well as their potential to provide farmers with a more affordable alternative to some conventional agricultural inputs. After the signing, Jospong Group Chief Investment and Innovation Officer Noah Gyimah said the company would work with Ghana’s environmental and standards authorities to ensure the products meet local regulatory requirements before introducing them for use on its farms. “Our joint efforts will transition this technology from research and development to practical application. We will commence with collaborative research and field trials in Ghana, followed by technology transfer and full-scale commercial production,” he said. Mr Gyimah said the pilot would also help AAC assess the commercial viability of the products, identify potential buyers and determine whether Ghana has sufficient raw materials to support local production. He said the consortium intends to make the products available to smallholder farmers if the trials establish their suitability. AAC also plans to assess their potential use in growing its own crops and vegetables on a commercial scale for the Ghanaian market. The agreement followed a visit by a four-member AAC delegation, led by the consortium’s Coordinator, Dr Emmanuel Volsuuri, to ChitoGlobal’s facility in Antalya. Dr Volsuuri said he arranged the visit after meeting the company at its COP31 pavilion, where further discussions led to the opportunity to examine its operations and technology first-hand. The delegation toured the facility to learn about the composition of the products and the operations of the company’s laboratories. Dr Volsuuri said the visit helped AAC assess the products’ potential to support crop disease management and improve soil health in Ghana. He also cited concerns about the widespread use of conventional chemical treatments in agriculture and the need to explore alternatives that could reduce farmers’ reliance on them. AAC Chief Executive, Dr Adelaide Araba Siaw Agyepong, leads the consortium, which grows rice, maize, vegetables and soybeans commercially in Ghana. The company also supports farmers with access to mechanisation services, financing and markets. ChitoGlobal Biotechnology develops biopolymer products for agricultural and medical applications. ChitoGlobal Sales and Technical Support Manager, Dana Abourahma, said the partnership would combine the expertise of both organisations. “This collaboration brings together extensive local knowledge with cutting-edge scientific capabilities,” she said. The proposed research and field trials will determine whether the chitosan-based products can be adapted for Ghanaian farms and whether local production could be commercially viable.

items.title: Haruna Iddrisu announces €325m loan plan to address water shortages in three Northern cities
items.description: Education Minister and Tamale South MP, Haruna Iddrisu, says a €325 million loan agreement to support water infrastructure projects in Tamale, Damongo and Yendi will be laid before Parliament next week. He made the announcement at a ceremony in Tamale organised by members of Ahlussunna wal Jama’a (ASWAJ) to celebrate the selection of Sheikh Ibrahim Basha Iddris, popularly known as Sheikh Bayaan, as the group’s interim National Imam. Addressing the gathering, Mr Iddrisu said Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson would present the agreement to Parliament. “Next week, the Finance Minister, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, will lay before Parliament a loan agreement of 325 million euros to end the water crisis in Tamale, Damongo, and Yendi,” he said. The proposed financing is expected to support major water infrastructure development in the three municipalities, where residents have experienced persistent challenges with reliable water supply. If approved by Parliament, the loan would provide funding for the planned interventions, although details of the project components, implementation timeline and expected completion dates were not provided in the announcement. The proposed investment is intended to improve access to potable water for households, businesses and public institutions in the beneficiary communities. Iddrisu welcomes Sheikh Bayaan’s selection The Education Minister also described Sheikh Bayaan’s selection as interim National Imam of ASWAJ as a significant moment for the organisation and the wider Muslim community. He expressed hope that the new leader’s tenure would contribute to the advancement of Islamic education in Ghana. “The choice of Sheikh Bayaan to lead ASWAJ as National Imam is a proud moment, and I am hopeful that his reign will be remembered for his enormous contribution to Islamic education in the country,” he said. The ceremony brought together members of ASWAJ in Tamale, who gathered to celebrate Sheikh Bayaan and pledge their allegiance to his leadership.

items.title: PSHAN, WHO urge increased private investment to rescue Nigeria’s healthcare system
items.description: By Matthew Johnson The Private Sector Health Alliance of Nigeria (PSHAN) and the World Health Organisation (WHO) have called for increased private sector investment and stronger public-private partnerships to address persistent challenges confronting Nigeria’s healthcare system. The organisations said government alone could not shoulder the responsibility of transforming the health sector, stressing that sustained private sector investment was critical to improving healthcare delivery, strengthening infrastructure and achieving universal health coverage. The call was made at the 2026 PSHAN Annual Gala and Awards Night held in Lagos on November 20, with the theme, “Legacy Builders: Honouring the Visionaries of the Nigerian Healthcare System.” Speaking at the event, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of PSHAN, Dr. Tinuola Akinbolagbe, said the alliance was working to position the private sector at the centre of Nigeria’s health development through strategic partnerships, investment, innovation and institutional strengthening. She said PSHAN was seeking to move beyond fragmented private sector interventions towards coordinated investments capable of strengthening health systems and delivering measurable and sustainable outcomes. According to her, meaningful progress in healthcare requires shared responsibility and collaboration across different sectors. “As we look towards 2027 and beyond, our ambition is to move from fragmented contributions by the private sector to coordinated investment, from isolated interventions to stronger health systems, and from good intentions to measurable, sustainable outcomes,” she said. Akinbolagbe explained that the theme of the event was designed to celebrate individuals, institutions and organisations whose courage, leadership, innovation and commitment had contributed to shaping the future of healthcare in Nigeria. In his keynote address, former President of the African Development Bank Group and Executive Chairman of the Global Africa Investment Summit, Dr. Akinwumi Adesina, described healthcare as an investment in human capital and essential economic infrastructure rather than merely social sector expenditure. Speaking on the theme, “Health as Wealth: Mobilising African Leadership and Capital to Build Sustainable Health Systems,” Adesina said a healthy population was fundamental to productivity, innovation, economic competitiveness and national prosperity. He maintained that no country could achieve sustainable wealth without a healthy population, insisting that investment in healthcare was essential to building a productive workforce and inclusive economy. Adesina called for stronger partnerships between government and the private sector, noting that government alone could not finance and deliver the transformation required in the country’s healthcare system. He urged businesses to move beyond philanthropy and corporate social responsibility initiatives to embrace healthcare as a strategic investment priority. “I urge businesses to move beyond philanthropy and corporate social responsibility initiatives to regard healthcare as a strategic investment priority. “Investments should be directed towards strengthening primary healthcare, training and supporting health workers, local production of essential medicines and vaccines, digital healthcare infrastructure, reliable diagnostics and sustainable health financing,” he said. The former AfDB president said Nigeria must build a healthcare system where women did not die during childbirth because of lack of access to quality medical services and families were not pushed into poverty by illness. He urged stakeholders to prioritise women, children and vulnerable communities, stressing that access to quality healthcare should not depend on an individual’s income or circumstances. “Nigeria must reduce its dependence on imported essential medicines, vaccines and diagnostic products by strengthening local manufacturing, promoting health innovation and developing resilient healthcare supply chains,” he added. Also speaking, Dr. Pavel Ursu, representing the World Health Organisation, warned that Nigeria and other African countries risked losing the benefits of their growing youthful populations without deliberate investments in healthcare. He identified high maternal and child mortality, inadequate healthcare funding, shortages of health workers and poor infrastructure as major challenges undermining the continent’s healthcare ambitions. Ursu stressed that healthcare facilities required essential infrastructure, including reliable electricity and water supply, to deliver quality services. He cited Nigeria’s Universal Health Coverage Compact, signed in December 2023 and expanded in 2025 to include the private sector, as an example of the importance of involving businesses in health policy development and implementation. He also identified the incorporation of the private sector into the implementation of the Basic Health Care Provision Fund as an opportunity to strengthen collaboration. “Government policies must encourage private sector participation. The responsibility of developing the health sector cannot be left to government alone,” he said. Ursu maintained that Africa’s demographic advantage could translate into a productive workforce and economic growth only if governments and other stakeholders took practical steps to improve health outcomes. Similarly, the Special Adviser to the President on Health, Dr. Salma Ibrahim-Anas, said the Federal Government had urged the organised private sector to deepen collaboration with public health institutions to translate national health policies into measurable improvements in the lives of Nigerians. She outlined six priority areas for private sector alignment under the Nigerian Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative. These include primary healthcare revitalisation, expansion of national health insurance enrolment, domestic manufacturing of pharmaceuticals and medical equipment, digital health deployment in underserved communities, maternal and child survival, and health workforce training. Citing 2026 Federal Ministry of Health statistics, Ibrahim-Anas disclosed that the private sector already contributed over N5 trillion to healthcare delivery, owned 82 per cent of secondary health facilities and had revamped more than 5,400 primary healthcare centres. She called on corporate organisations to move beyond isolated corporate social responsibility projects towards integrated investments aligned with state and local government priorities under the sector-wide approach. She warned against abandoned and poorly equipped healthcare projects, stressing that renovated facilities must be adequately staffed and supplied with essential medicines, electricity and water. “Private sector healthcare spending should be viewed as a strategic investment in human capital, workforce productivity and national economic growth rather than mere charity,” she said. The United Nations Under-Secretary-General and Special Adviser on Africa, Dr. Ahunna Eziakonwa, also urged private sector leaders and policymakers to move beyond isolated health interventions and build enduring partnerships capable of strengthening public healthcare delivery for future generations. Eziakonwa said the theme, “Legacy Builders: Honouring the Visionaries of Nigerian Healthcare,” represented the importance of building sustainable institutions that continuously improve lives rather than measuring legacies merely by physical structures or accumulated wealth. She noted that governments had the primary responsibility of setting standards, financing public services and protecting equity, but maintained that private sector capital, technology and operational expertise could achieve greater impact when aligned with national, state and local health priorities. “Cross-sector partnerships remain critical to Africa’s broader economic transformation, food security and climate resilience. Corporate and public leaders must sustain long-term alliances that deliver quality healthcare across generations,” she said. The awards ceremony featured 125 public nominations across five major categories and 25 subcategories, which were subsequently reduced to 75 through public voting. The organisers said the awards were designed to celebrate excellence across Nigeria’s healthcare ecosystem while encouraging greater commitment to sustainable healthcare development. The post PSHAN, WHO urge increased private investment to rescue Nigeria’s healthcare system appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Who wants Odegbami dead? By Segun Odegbami
items.description: The Bible told us that the Jebusites were descendants of Canaan, the son of Ham. An ancient Canaanite tribe who inhabited the hill country and fortified stronghold of Jebus, later known as Jerusalem. They were among the peoples inhabiting the land God promised to Abraham’s descendants and Moses. They derive their name from a Hebrew root meaning “thresher,” “to trample down,” or “to tread on”. Breaking this further down spiritually, “the name denotes a force that “stomps” or grinds down others, attempting to minimize, humiliate, or crush a person’s potential and authority”. I have used the above to explain the situation we have in the administration of football in Nigeria since a certain group of human hyenas took control of the running of the game by ‘forcefully’ truncating the second term of one of Nigeria’s renowned sports administrators, Alhaji Ibrahim Galadima in 2006. Alhaji Galadima, now late, wanted a reform of the Nigeria Football Association’s (NFA ) laws that excluded the majority of football’s key stakeholders. After successfully getting the Kano-born administrator out of their way, the football ‘Jebusites’ changed NFA into NFF (Nigeria Football Federation) and manipulated the statutes to give more voting powers to the State FA Chairmen. One stakeholder who would not rest until a proper reform was carried out for an inclusive Congress that would allow other stakeholders an opportunity to help change the face of football in Nigeria is Chief Segun Odegbami. He used his weekly Column syndicated in some Nigerian newspapers for the campaign. He made speeches at seminars and sports workshops to spread his message for the reform of the NFF to no avail. Nigerians carried on as if all was well with our football. A handful of Nigerians, sports journalists and passionate fans, joined in the crusade but their ‘cries’ seemed not to make any impact as the football Jebusites who seemed to enjoy the support of the government carried on. Still Odegbami would not be deterred. His campaign intensified and went wide when he established a radio station, Eagle7 FM based in his little rustic town of Mosimi in Ogun State of Nigeria. He talked about the rot in football and assembled analysts regularly to talk about why a reform is desirable before it causes Nigeria’s football to go into the ICU- Intensive Care Unit. Odegbami is not a prophet of doom like Jeremiah and Ezekiel in the Bible who predicted gloom for Israel if the leaders didn’t do the right things, but his fears for football eventually came to pass. Nigeria’s football prospects declined and all her teams, from ‘top to bottom’, apologies late President Muhammad Buhari, began to crash, surprisingly against minnows of yesterday. Despite this, the Jebusites were climbing on both CAF and FIFA profile ladders and smiling. At this stage, Odegbami’s campaign began to make sense to Nigerian fans who depended on the success of our football teams to console themselves in the midst of the unending economic crunch that had put them under physical and emotional stress. And at last the government thought it was high time it looked into the simmering crisis in football and how it could be stemmed. When the Jebusites saw the stand of the government, they talked to themselves and step aside. Although some people still believe that they were forced to throw in the towel. Their mass resignation led to the decision by CAF and FIFA to step in and today a 5-man Normalisation Committee has been appointed to start the process of repositioning football with a reform that would allow a level playing field for all stakeholders. With the Committee in place, it has become clear to the Jebusites that the end to their vice-grip on football has come to an end and that the era of deciding who could be elected into the NFF Board and become the president has gone. Not quite a week after FIFA announced the Normalisation Committee, armed men invaded the Abeokuta home of the champion for the reform process in football, Chief Odegbami and nearly snuffed life out of him. I don’t want to believe that those who are not happy that they lost their juicy positions in the NFF because of Odegbami’s consistent campaigns are behind this dastardly act. An African adage which says, ‘the witch cried last night and the child died today’ that has kept me thinking since the news of the attack on Odegbami broke. Odegbami has been a very easy going man, living for his former teammates, creating opportunities for them whenever he has a sports or football project to carry out for the good of the country. They were involved in the Shell Cup for secondary schools he coordinated with the support of Shell Petroleum and Development Company as sponsor and the Nigeria School Sports Federation, NSSF as the organising body. He still involves them to run his Segun Odegbami International College & Sports Academy (SOCA). They are among analysts he features frequently on the Eagle7 FM radio to dissect the problems of sports and proffer solutions that could make Nigerian athletes excel. Would anyone say that the man, who uses his money and connections to assist his colleagues and help make things work for the progress of our athletes, hates Nigeria? That is why I ask today, who wants Odegbami dead? The police must get to the root of the assassination attempt on him, fish out the culprits and bring them to justice. A man like Odegbami who has had sleepless nights thinking of how the Super Eagles could be great again with a proper running of the NFF should not be the target of wicked people and must be protected by the country. Chief Odegbami, here is wishing you a quick recovery from that deadly machete cut which could have snuffed life out of you. The post Who wants Odegbami dead? By Segun Odegbami appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Anambra’s Ekwulobia flyover to be commissioned November 27
items.description: By Vincent Ujumadu The Anambra State Executive Council has fixed November 27, 2026, for the formal commissioning and opening of the Ekwulobia flyover constructed by the administration of Governor Chukwuma Soludo. The flyover is strategically located at a junction that previously experienced serious traffic challenges, particularly during festive periods when vehicular movement increases significantly. Rising from its meeting in Awka, the State Executive Council directed that all necessary arrangements be made to ensure a successful and hitch-free commissioning. However, it did not disclose who would perform the ceremony. The state Commissioner for Information and Value Reorientation, Dr Law Mefor, described the flyover as one of the flagship urban regeneration projects of the Soludo administration. He said the project stood alongside the transformation of Okpoko, formerly regarded as the biggest urban slum in the South-East, into an area characterised by improved infrastructure, order and human dignity. “These projects underscore Governor Soludo’s irreversible commitment to building a liveable, prosperous and smart mega-city in Anambra State,” Mefor said. Meanwhile, the Council resolved to move the state’s Internally Generated Revenue (IGR) drive from moral suasion to full enforcement, including the prosecution of tax evaders, to maximise the state’s revenue potential. It consequently urged residents, business owners and other taxpayers to pay their taxes and levies promptly to avoid the consequences of enforcement, particularly prosecution. According to the Council, no modern state can be built on voluntary compliance alone, stressing that payment of taxes is a civic responsibility. “Anambra will enforce it fairly and firmly,” the Council said. The Council also disclosed that it had concluded work on the state’s 2027 budget, which Governor Soludo is expected to present to the Anambra State House of Assembly on Tuesday. Mefor described the proposed budget as a consolidation budget designed to deepen the gains of Solution 2.0 in infrastructure, security, education, healthcare, youth empowerment and economic transformation.
