items.title: ‘A tray of locust beans’ come to the screen, by Bisi Adeleye-Fayemi
items.description: I watched the first cut of the 50-minute film at the Lufodo Productions office at Glover Hall in May. I cried. I wrote ‘A Tray of Locust Beans’ ten years ago. I have met many Mabels over the years and I have worked with others to ensure that they do not fall through the many cracks in our communities. Sadly, demand always exceeds supply, and there are too many Mabels and not enough of a support system to break the cycle of poverty and oppression decisively. My dear friend and sister Ajoke Silva, founder of Lufodo Productions, persuaded me to look into making some of my stories or poems into short films. I have always believed that advocacy efforts need to take many forms so that they can be relevant to as many spaces as possible. When I wrote ‘A Tray of Locust Beans’, I wanted to draw attention to the pervasive nature of sexual exploitation of poor young girls. By making this into a film, I hope that people can locate themselves somewhere along the spectrum of support required to enable us have better outcomes for young people around us. Lufodo Productions was commissioned by Amandla Institute for Policy and Leadership Advancement and Above Whispers Media Foundation to make the film, and it was directed by Orobosa Ikponmwen. ‘A Tray of Locust Beans’ was selected for screening at the African International Film Festival (AFRIFF), and it was shown on November 5th. The response to the film has been overwhelmingly positive. We were even shortlisted for Best Short Film at AFRIFF! There was a panel discussion after the screening on November 5th, which featured the production crew as well as sexual violence and child protection specialists. We have laws and policies in place, but more needs to be done to make the relevant institutions and duty bearers functional and accountable. There will be another screening in Abuja on December 1st, during the annual 16 Days of Activism against Gender Based Violence campaign, then it will be released for public viewing. I thank everyone who has been a part of making this project a success. My deep appreciation to The Ford Foundation for their support. We cannot continue to lose young girls just because they are poor and have limited choices. This means the next generation of potential Lawyers, Doctors, Engineers and Professors will end up with trays on their heads, while the boys and men who put them in this predicament go through life with minimal consequences. We all need to do more. For those who have not read the story before, here it is. The person sitting next to Mabel nudged her. Her name was being called. She hadn’t been listening. Her mind was far away. Many years away. She had been thinking about the pain. She had often wondered how it was possible for any human being to survive that kind of pain. Then her mind wandered even further back to how she got to be in pain in the first place. A few weeks after her twelfth birthday, she noticed some blood on her panties. Her grandmother, Mama, had told her this would happen one day.She had been told, ‘Soon you will become a woman. You will bleed every month. This means you have to stay away from boys’. She was not told why she had to stay away from boys, and she did not want to ask because she did not want to upset Mama. She did not know when ‘soon’ would come, so she decided not to worry about it. Then her period came and she had to go and tell Mama. Mama and her older sister Mary, were the only relatives she was close to. The others were in distant places and like strangers. Mabel and Mary’s parents had died in a car accident, five years before. Mary was sent to live with a relative in Ibadan while Mabel lived with their paternal grandmother in Akure. Mama sold provisions as well as locust beans known locally as ‘Iru’. In the afternoon after shereturned from school, she hawked some of Mama’s locust beans. Then Mama fell ill and could not go to her shop.Mabel had to hawk the Irufor longer hours than she used to. One day, Mr Felix, the tailor who lived two streets away, called her in to his room to sell him some Iru. He then pinned her down and forced himself on her. He covered her mouth to prevent her from screaming. When he was done, he gave her N200 and warned her not to tell anyone. Mabel was too scared to let anyone know, and besides Mama who was ill and had her own worries, there was no one to tell anything. Mary was not there. Mabel kept hawking her Iru after school, but made sure she did not pass by Mr Felix’s house.Soon, things got very bad for Mama and Mabel. Therewas no money in the house for them to buy food, and even when they had something to cook, Mabel had to do it because Mama was unable to. Mabel stopped going to school, so that she could look after Mama and sell Iru.Sinawas three years older than her. He was in her school as well and hawked bread for his mother. He was very kind to her. He gave her some of his bread to eat, and would lie to his mother that he lost one or two loaves when he tripped and fell with his tray, or a policeman had forcefully taken one from him. She liked being with Sina because he made her laugh and she looked forward to his company. After what Mr Felix had done to her, she now understood what Mama had said about staying away from boys, but she thought to herself, ‘Sina is a good boy. He will never hurt me like Mr Felix’. When Sina kissed her, she did not push him away, and when he lifted her dress, she did not stop him. It felt good to be with him. He was her only friend and she did not want to hurt him. That meant he would stop talking to her, and she might even go hungry if he did not give her the bread she had become accustomed to. A few weeks after she had started going to the abandoned house in their neighborhood with Sina, she was stopped by Mr Jasper, a policeman who always seemed to be in a bad mood. He asked her to follow him, and since she was too afraid to ask where to or why, she obediently went with him. He took her to his house and did the same thing Mr Felix had done. This time, she did not cry. When he allowed her to leave, she turned to him and said, ‘You need to give me N1,000’. ‘Why?’ he asked her. ‘That is what a full tray of Iru costs. I need to explain to Mama where I have been and why I have not sold my Iru.’ He gave her the money. It became a routine. Locust beawns. Bread. Sina.Mr Jasper. Then she became pregnant. By now, Mama was feeling better, and was able to move about. Mama wailed and shouted for everyone to hear, ‘Who has impregnated a thirteen year old girl? What kind of monster has done this’? Mama asked her who was responsible, and after a lot of beating and threats, she named Mr Jasper as the culprit. She was silent about Mr Felix and Sina. When Mama went to see Mr Jasper about the matter, predictably, she was threatened with arrest, a beating, and even death. One of their neighbours who was a teacher, Auntie Cecilia, advised Mama to go and see Lawyer Tina who usually helped with cases such as this. Lawyer Tina was a smart, immaculately dressed woman, who drove a shiningblack car. She spoke English as if she had been speaking it from the day she was born and she spoke so quickly, sometimes Mabel did not understand her. Mabel had never seen any woman like her, not even her teachers in school. Lawyer Tina responded quickly. She took her to the Ministry for Women. They declared that Mama was an ‘incompetent’ guardian. Mabel did not know what ‘incompetent’ meant. The Ministry said she would either have to go and live with another relative, or go to the government rehabilitation center.Mama did not want her sent to relatives far away, so she agreed when Lawyer Tina offered to look after her as a temporary guardian. Mabel liked Lawyer Tina, because she talked to her about a lot of things and answered all her questions without scolding her like Mama. Lawyer Tina had told her that they would wait till after her baby was born, and then do a ‘DNA test’ to determine if Mr Jasper was the father. If he was, he would go to prison. This made Mabel nervous. What if it was not Mr Jasper? She however knew she needed to say something. The longer she waited, the more trouble she would be in. She eventually found the courage to confide in Lawyer Tina. Her reaction shocked her. She expected Lawyer Tina to scream at her and call her a prostitute,useless and wicked, and beat her like Mama had done. Instead, Lawyer Tina burst into tears and hugged her tight. She called her a victim and said that that she had been ‘explooted’. She had her baby after a lot of pain. That was the pain she was thinking about when she was nudged out of her reverie. She was in labour for many hours, till Lawyer Tina insisted that they perform an operation. ‘You can’t expect a thirteen year old to push a baby out’ she yelled at the Doctors. Lawyer Tina took her case to Mrs Kitara, the Governor’s Wife, who decided to adopt her. She would remain under the guardianship of Lawyer Tina, but all her expenses would be covered by her new benefactor. Her sister Mary was brought back from Ibadan to stay with her in a new apartment that was arranged by Mrs Kitara. Mabel was in awe of Mrs Kitara too, a kind lady who also spoke like Lawyer Tina – plenty of English and very fast. She also smelt very nice. Mabel day dreamed of how, one day, she would be like them. The applause continued as Mabel stood up and walked towards the stage in the auditorium. The Vice-Chancellor shook her hand and presented her with a special plaque as Best Graduating Student, Faculty of Law. Even though she could not see them, Mabel knew that Lawyer Tina, Mrs Kitara, Mary and her son Emmanuel, were in the audience. Mama was still alive, but too old to make the trip to attend her graduation.Mabel never found out who Emmanuel’s father was. Mr Felix skipped town and Mr Jasper was transferred to a state in the North. She never spoke to Sina again. All this was ten years ago. Now her dream had come true. She was going to be like Lawyer Tina and Mrs Kitara. Knowledgeable, articulate and successful. ‘I am here because of them’, she thought. ‘Young girls are exploited and abused every day. They did not judge me. They gave me opportunities. They saved my life. I will dedicate my life to helping others ‘, she silently promised herself. As she walked back to her seat clutching the plaque, she no longer remembered the pain. Only the hope she had been given. Bisi Adeleye-Fayemi is a Gender Specialist, Leadership Coach, Policy Advocate and Writer. She is the Founder of Abovewhispers.com, an online community for women. She can be reached at BAF@abovewhispers.com The post ‘A tray of locust beans’ come to the screen, by Bisi Adeleye-Fayemi appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Makinde’s image on campaign balloon stirs controversy at Tinubu’s Ibadan rally
items.description: By Adeola Badru The image of Oyo State Governor, Seyi Makinde, displayed alongside those of President Bola Tinubu and other political figures on a campaign balloon at the All Progressives Congress (APC) rally in Ibadan on Saturday has stirred controversy, raising questions about the governor’s political alignment ahead of the 2027 general elections. The balloon, hoisted at the rally ground around the historic Mapo Hall, featured images of prominent political figures, including Makinde, who is not a member of the APC and has yet to publicly declare support for Tinubu’s re-election bid. Its appearance attracted attention at the campaign venue, particularly as Makinde is the presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM). The governor’s inclusion on the balloon raised questions about the circumstances surrounding the display and the political message it was intended to convey. However, it was not immediately clear who authorised the inclusion of Makinde’s image or the circumstances that led to its appearance at the APC rally. Meanwhile, President Tinubu has urged residents of Oyo State to sustain their support for the APC, declaring that continuity was essential for Nigeria’s progress, prosperity and development. Speaking at the rally, Tinubu promised increased investments in education, agriculture, industrialisation and electricity supply, while endorsing Senator Sharafadeen Alli as the APC’s governorship candidate in the state. The President also announced plans to revive the old Leyland factory in Ibadan, disclosing that his administration had signed an agreement with Chinese automobile manufacturer, Yutong, to reopen the facility for public transport vehicle production and establish an automobile assembly plant. “For Oyo State, we have just signed an agreement with China’s Yutong to reopen the old Leyland factory in Ibadan. We are reopening it to produce public transport vehicles and establish an automobile assembly plant there. We will continue to bring industries. You will see progress and development,” Tinubu said. He also assured residents of improved electricity supply, expressing confidence in the efforts of the Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, and his team. “You will see, and I guarantee you an improvement in electricity. Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe is really working hard with his team,” he said. Tinubu urged the electorate to remain committed to the APC, recalling their support for the party in the previous election. “You voted overwhelmingly for APC last time. You must stay the course. You must. For the sake of progress, prosperity of our country, development, for your children and our great-grandchildren,” he said. He stressed the need to prioritise education and agriculture to create opportunities for younger generations. “We must give them the right education, invest in agriculture,” he said. The President also criticised opposition parties, describing them as “mediocre”, and urged voters not to be distracted by them. He subsequently endorsed Alli for the 2027 governorship election, urging the people of Oyo State to vote for him. “I will show you the governorship candidate in Oyo State that you must vote for, and is Sen. Sharafadeen Alli,” Tinubu said. Traditional rulers receive Tinubu The rally was preceded by the President’s arrival at the Ladoke Akintola Airport, Ibadan, where the Olubadan of Ibadanland, Oba Rashidi Ladoja, and other traditional rulers received him. The monarchs, drawn from the Ibadan, Ibarapa, Oyo, Ogbomoso and Oke-Ogun zones, reaffirmed their support for Tinubu’s re-election bid. Welcoming the President on behalf of the Oyo State Council of Obas and Chiefs, Ladoja described Tinubu as the leader the traditional rulers had been waiting to receive. “This is the President and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu that we have been waiting for,” the Olubadan said. The monarch commended the President for infrastructure projects across the country, particularly in the South-West, citing the Leyland Motor Assembly project, the Ibadan-Ijebu-Ode Road and the Ibadan-Oyo Road. He, however, urged the Federal Government to ensure the completion of ongoing projects before embarking on additional ones. Tinubu thanked the monarchs for their prayers and cooperation, urging them to encourage their subjects to participate in the forthcoming election. The President also observed a minute’s silence in honour of victims of a boat accident in Bayelsa State, expressing sympathy with their bereaved families. Gunshots, panic at rally Earlier, tension had erupted at the rally venue as hoodlums clashed before the President’s arrival, with gunshots reportedly fired into the air. The incident triggered panic among supporters, many of whom scampered for safety as the situation deteriorated. Some of the hoodlums were seen dragging a firearm reportedly used by an unidentified man, while others hurled sticks and placards towards the media stand, disrupting activities at the venue. The clash led to the dispersal of parts of the crowd and briefly disrupted preparations for the President’s arrival. items.title: From global blacklist to international recognition: Tinubu’s unprecedented aviation transformation
items.description: By Seyi Bakare 91.45% ICAO safety rating breaks all previous records; five international airports achieve full certification; $850m trapped airline funds cleared; Emirates returns; indigenous airlines empowered as massive infrastructure renewal takes off. Nigeria’s aviation industry is undergoing one of the most remarkable transformations in its history, with the administration of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu recording unprecedented milestones in aviation safety, airport infrastructure, international relations, airline operations and the restoration of investor confidence. What was once an industry struggling with international credibility, restricted access to aircraft financing, trapped foreign airline revenues, deteriorating infrastructure and regulatory deficiencies is gradually emerging as a more competitive and internationally respected aviation destination. The transformation is not merely reflected in government announcements or policy pronouncements. It is increasingly evident in measurable improvements in safety oversight, the return of major international airlines, renewed access to aircraft leasing markets, the expansion of indigenous carriers and substantial investments in airport infrastructure across the country. Perhaps the most compelling evidence of this turnaround is Nigeria’s historic 91.45 per cent Effective Implementation score in the International Civil Aviation Organisation’s (ICAO) safety oversight assessment conducted in April 2026. The achievement represents Nigeria’s highest aviation safety rating in history, placing the country significantly above the global average of 70.4 per cent and the West African regional average of 61.1 per cent. It is a remarkable departure from the approximately 70 per cent performance that had characterised previous assessments. For an industry where safety standards determine international confidence, investment decisions and operational credibility, the improvement represents a significant national achievement. The administration has also achieved full aerodrome certification of Nigeria’s five international airports in Lagos, Abuja, Kano, Port Harcourt and Enugu for the first time in the country’s history. These accomplishments demonstrate the impact of deliberate regulatory reforms, institutional strengthening and investments in modern aviation infrastructure. Rebuilding Nigeria’s aviation gateways Beyond regulatory improvements, the Tinubu administration has embarked on an ambitious programme to modernise the country’s airport infrastructure. The flagship project is the comprehensive reconstruction and modernisation of Terminal 1 at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos, with a Federal Government commitment of N712.3 billion. The project, which is more than 50 per cent complete as of November 2026, is designed to transform Nigeria’s busiest international gateway into a modern aviation facility capable of meeting contemporary international standards The scope includes redesigned passenger movement systems, modern baggage handling facilities, a new overhead bridge and a skywalk connecting passengers to the departure halls of Terminals 1 and 2. Significantly, the project is being financed through the Renewed Hope Infrastructure Development Fund, using savings from subsidy reforms rather than new external borrowing. In Kano, N46 billion has been committed to the resurfacing of the runway at the Mallam Aminu Kano International Airport. The domestic terminal has also been completely remodelled, while a new Hajj terminal was commissioned in July 2026. The administration has equally supported the upgrading of the Muhammadu Buhari Airport in Maiduguri to full international status, including a new international terminal and facilities for immigration, customs and other relevant agencies. Other notable interventions include the upgrading of Victor Attah International Airport in Uyo to full international operations, the rehabilitation and expansion of the Benin Airport terminal, the provision of runway lighting at Osubi Airport, the construction of a new terminal at Akure Airport and the ongoing runway expansion programme at Sam Mbakwe International Cargo Airport, Owerri. The Federal Government has also approved the development of a new international airport at Ubaha Nsulu in Abia State. These projects reflect an emerging national aviation network in which more states can participate meaningfully in international commerce, tourism, cargo transportation and investment. Restoring international confidence One of the most significant achievements of the Tinubu administration has been its success in addressing the crisis of trapped airline funds that threatened Nigeria’s international aviation relationships. At its peak in June 2023, foreign airlines had approximately $850 million in revenues trapped in Nigerian banks because of foreign exchange liquidity challenges. The situation was so serious that some international airlines suspended operations, while others threatened to withdraw from the Nigerian market. Through coordinated intervention by the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Ministry of Aviation and Aerospace Development, the backlog was substantially cleared by mid-2024. The International Air Transport Association subsequently acknowledged the progress, while Nigeria was removed from the list of countries with blocked airline funds. As of November 2026, Nigeria has emerged as Africa’s leading country in the repatriation of airline funds. Another significant diplomatic and aviation milestone was the return of Emirates Airlines to Nigeria on October 1, 2024, after suspending operations in 2022. The resumption followed high-level diplomatic engagements between Nigeria and the United Arab Emirates, culminating in a renewed bilateral aviation agreement. The return of Emirates restored an important international connection and demonstrated renewed confidence in Nigeria’s aviation market Breaking the aircraft leasing barrier For years, Nigerian airlines faced enormous difficulties accessing aircraft through international leasing arrangements. Nigeria’s poor compliance standing under the Cape Town Convention had placed the country on the Aviation Working Group’s non-compliance watchlist, making international lessors reluctant to expose their aircraft to the Nigerian market. The Tinubu administration addressed this challenge through legal and regulatory reforms, including the signing of a Practice Direction by the Chief Judge of the Federal High Court in 2024 and the operationalisation of the Irrevocable De-registration and Export Request Authorisation (IDERA). Consequently, Nigeria’s compliance score improved from 49.5 per cent to 75.5 per cent, leading to its removal from the Aviation Working Group’s watchlist. The practical benefit became evident when Air Peace secured a Boeing 737-700 NG on dry lease from AerCap, one of the world’s leading aircraft leasing companies. To consolidate this achievement, the Federal Executive Council approved the establishment of the Nigeria Aircraft Leasing Company in April 2026. The initiative, which is fully privately funded, is projected to unlock more than $1 billion in aircraft financing capacity for Nigerian airlines through a locally based special-purpose vehicle supported by limited government guarantees. This is a potentially transformative intervention for indigenous carriers that have historically paid significantly higher aircraft leasing costs than their international competitors. Strengthening indigenous airlines The administration has also demonstrated a clear commitment to strengthening Nigerian-owned airlines. Rather than proceeding with the controversial inherited national carrier arrangement involving Ethiopian Airlines, which faced significant legal challenges, the government discontinued the proposed structure and redirected attention towards supporting existing indigenous operators. Air Peace’s entry into the Lagos-London route in March 2024 was a significant demonstration of this policy direction. The airline subsequently expanded its London operations to include Abuja, with services to Heathrow and Gatwick following diplomatic engagements with the United Kingdom. Approval has also been secured for the proposed Owerri-Lagos-London and London-Owerri operations, further strengthening the international aviation prospects of the South-East. In April 2026, President Tinubu also approved a 30 per cent discount on outstanding debts owed by domestic airlines to aviation agencies, following concerns over rising aviation fuel costs and threats of operational shutdowns. These interventions, alongside engagements with major aircraft manufacturers including Boeing, Airbus, Embraer and Bombardier, are aimed at creating a more favourable operating environment for Nigerian carriers. Ending two decades of legal uncertainty Another major achievement is the resolution of the nearly two-decade dispute between the Federal Government and Bi-Courtney Aviation Services Limited over the operation of Murtala Muhammed Airport Terminal 2. The prolonged disagreement had denied the Federal Government expected revenue from the terminal for almost twenty years and created considerable uncertainty around the public-private partnership arrangement. Following approval by the Federal Executive Council in April 2026, a negotiated settlement was finally signed in October 2026. The resolution represents an important breakthrough in the management of aviation infrastructure and provides a clearer framework for investment and operational responsibilities. Building aviation expertise and creating local value The administration has also moved to strengthen Nigeria’s aviation human capital through the commencement of full operations at the African Aviation and Aerospace University in Abuja. The institution is expected to develop specialised manpower in aviation management, engineering and regulatory studies, reducing the country’s dependence on expensive foreign training institutions. Similarly, the government’s policy requiring international airlines operating in Nigeria to source onboard meals for outbound flights from local caterers has created new opportunities for indigenous businesses. The impact is becoming visible in the expansion of local aviation catering companies, including the opening of a N10 billion catering facility in Abuja in October 2026. The administration has equally approved approximately N36 billion for the payment of pensions and severance benefits to more than 3,300 former employees of the defunct Nigeria Airways, with an initial N18 billion already released. This represents a long-awaited resolution of an outstanding obligation that had lingered for more than two decades. Nigeria’s rising international aviation profile Perhaps one of the strongest indications of the country’s improved aviation standing is the growing international recognition of its leadership and regulatory achievements. The Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, SAN, was named among Africa’s top four aviation figures by the International Air Transport Association in April 2026. He was also appointed Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the Banjul Accord Group, a regional aviation organisation promoting harmonised safety oversight and regulatory standards among West African countries. Furthermore, the African Development Bank appointed him champion of its $7 billion Integrated Aviation Transformation Programme for Africa, with Nigeria as a pilot country. Nigeria also hosted its first-ever International Airshow in December 2025, attracting international aircraft manufacturers, lessors, airlines and other aviation stakeholders. For a country that had previously struggled with international aircraft leasing restrictions, hosting such an event was a powerful demonstration of its renewed ambition and growing relevance in the global aviation community. A new chapter for Nigerian aviation Taken together, these developments represent a significant departure from the challenges that confronted Nigeria’s aviation industry in 2023. The record-breaking ICAO safety score, the certification of all five international airports, the return of Emirates, the clearance of trapped airline funds, improved aircraft leasing opportunities, support for indigenous carriers and the extensive airport modernisation programme constitute important milestones in the industry’s development. While challenges relating to operating costs, passenger experience, infrastructure delivery and airline sustainability remain, the foundations for a more competitive and internationally respected aviation sector are increasingly being established. The significance of President Tinubu’s intervention lies not simply in the number of projects undertaken, but in the deliberate effort to address structural weaknesses that had constrained the industry for years. From regulatory credibility to international partnerships, from airport infrastructure to indigenous airline development, Nigeria’s aviation sector is witnessing a major institutional and operational reset. The journey is far from complete, but one thing is increasingly evident: Nigeria is reclaiming its place in the international aviation community, and the Tinubu administration’s reforms are providing the foundation for that renewed ambition. Bakare sent this piece through seyibakre@aol.com The post From global blacklist to international recognition: Tinubu’s unprecedented aviation transformation appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Praises provoke miracles, by Funmi Komolafe
items.description: Beloved, let’s thank God that we are gradually moving to the end of 2026. May the LORD see us to the end of the year joyfully in Jesus name. We might have heard of the eleventh hour miracle which some have interpreted to mean the miracle that happens when hope is lost. It is miracle when the benefactor does not expect it. When a woman gets pregnant at age 63 or any age after 45, it is a last minute miracle. It could also be miracle that one does not deserve but got one because of the mercy of God. An example is the labourer that was hired when work was almost completed but got the same pay as those that had worked their hearts out. Matthew 16 vs. 8-11: (KJV)“ So when even was come, the lord of the vineyard saith unto his steward, Call the labourers, and give them their hire, beginning from the last unto the first. And when they came that were hired about the eleventh hour, they received every man a penny. But when the first came, they supposed that they should have received more; and they likewise received every man a penny. And when they had received it, they murmured against the good man of the house”. Brethren, when you receive an eleventh hour miracle, some people would grumble. They would express doubts, some might even be unhappy but they would be unable to stop the work of God. The labourer in the above quoted passage, got an eleventh hour miracle by the mercy of the master of the vineyard. You too can receive an eleventh hour miracle by the mercy of God. You can also provoke yours with Praises. How do I know? Psalm 22 vs. 3-4 gives me the answer. It states, “ But thou are holy, O thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel. Our fathers trusted in thee: they trusted, and thou didst deliver them”. When we praise God with faith, we should know that God would not watch you praise him and do nothing. The LORD would definitely take an action on your behalf when you praise Him. King David, the shepherd boy that God made a king also knew that God is moved to action when he is praised hence David wrote many Psalms of praise to God. Psalm 34 vs. 1-3 is my witness. “ I will bless the LORD at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth. My soul shall make her boast in the LORD; the humble shall hear therof, and be glad. O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together”. If you still have doubts, remember King Jehoshaphat used praises to provoke God to deal with enemies when three kings that were too strong for him rose against him. Like any human being, Jehoshaphat feared. He cried to God in prayer but his last instrument was Praise. 2 Chronicles 20 vs. 21 &22 tells us what happened. “ And when he had consulted with the people, he appointed singers unto the LORD, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army, and to say, Praise the LORD; for his mercy endureth for ever. And when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set ambushments against the children of Ammon, Moab, and mount Seir, which were come against Judah; and they were smitten”. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whoever gangs up against God’s plans for you, the LORD will smite them as He did to the enemies of Jehoshaphat. In the case of Jehoshaphat he raised a praise worship theme when he was confronted with enemies too strong for him to handle. In the case of David, he formed the habit of praising God always and he always had victory. Even when he committed sins, God still had mercy on him. Perhaps because he had a habit of praising God almost on a daily basis. 2 Kings 6 vs. 21 tells us more about what happened when David was praising God after a victory over his enemies. 2 Samuel 6 vs. 20-21: “ Then David returned to bless his household. And Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David, and said, How glorious was the king of Israel today in the eyes of the handmaids of his servants, as one of the vain fellows shamelessly uncovereth himself! And David said unto Michal, It was before the LORD, which chose me before thy father, and before all his house, to appoint me ruler over the people of the LORD, over Israel: therefore will I play before the LORD”. For rebuking David for praising God without protocol, see what the LORD did to Michal in verse 23. “ Therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child unto the day of her death”. This should tell us that the Almighty God takes Praises seriously. The question for us now, is when and how do we praise the LORD? Human beings tend to praise God when we have a testimony. When God has done something that gladdens us or when he has delivered us from any form of pain, sorrow or accidents etc we find it easy to praise the Lord. In such situations, praises flow from us freely. We begin to dance, shout , sing songs. This is in order but we can also praise God when we acknowledge what he has done in the past like the sinking of Pharaoh and his horse riders and other miracles. Brethren, the best time to praise God however is when we are expecting a miracle. That was the strategy of king Jehoshaphat and it worked for him. However, it takes a higher level of faith to praise the LORD when you are still expecting a miracle. It is an action taken to demonstrate total faith and confidence in the ability of God to do the impossible and to reverse the irreversible. It is a total demonstration of trust in God. My prayer for you today, is that it doesn’t matter what you are still looking forward to, the Holy Spirit will open your mouth to praise the LORD at all times. You need the Holy Spirit to help you because the flesh is bound to discourage you and give you the spiritual strength that you need to praise God in the time of need. You may then ask, how do I praise God when I am in my office or not in a church? There are several ways to praise God. For this article, we’ll discuss the names of God. Brethren, you don’t need to shout when you call the Lord by His names when you are in a place that is not convenient to do so. God has numerous names and each name, is for a purpose and all names are miracle working instrument. You only need to repeat the names until your spirit man picks it up. The numerous names of God, include, Jehovah El- Shadier, ( God Almighty), Jehovah Nissi, (Lord is my banner), the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, The God of all flesh, Jehovah Sabaoth ( The Lord of Hosts). Jehovah Jireh,( My Provider), Jehovah Rapha (The Lord that heals) , Jehovah Shalom ( The Lord is Peace), Others include, Jehovah Elohim ( The Creator), Jehovah Rohi ( The Lord my shepherd), Yaweh ( I AM) and many more. Brethren, whatever is your need, God can meet it. Beloved as the year winds down, may the Lord open your mouth to praise the LORD. God is good at all times. The post Praises provoke miracles, by Funmi Komolafe appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Nigerian politicians preparing for war, not election, by Dele Sobowale
items.description: “War is nothing more than the continuation of politics by other means” – Karl von Clausewitz, 1780-1831 The Prussian General and military theorist could not have had Nigeria in mind when he wrote several books on politics and war because Nigeria did not exist then. But, some of his theories, which are still required reading in military academies worldwide, apply to the Nigerian political situation at the moment. Several Nigerian leading scholars have argued, with a great deal of conviction, that our country’s progress has been retarded by lack of institutions. That may be so. But, the nation is drifting towards war in January precisely because the most important institutions governing elections and which are supposed to be the guard-rails of democracy don’t appear to be doing their job. The institutions I have in mind are INEC, police, DSS, EFCC and the judiciary. No ranking is implied in the listing. THE FIRST SHALL BE THE LAST– JUDICIARY “We must not regard political consequences, how formidable so ever they might be. If rebellion was certain consequence, we are bound to say: ‘Fiat Justitia caelum’ (Latin), meaning, ‘Let justice be done even if the world perishes’” – Lord Mansfield, VANGUARD BOOK OF QUOTATIONS, VBQ, p 112. One Federal High Court, FHC, Justice (name withheld), will serve proxy for what the Nigerian judiciary has become – even before retired Supreme Court Justice Augie informed us that the Nigerian court has become a cash and carry outfit. My Lord of the FHC has delivered at least two judgments which defy basic rules of justice. First, he made a pronouncement on a matter already before the Court of Appeal; and was roundly reprimanded. Second, he again made a contrary ruling on a matter on which another FHC had already given judgment. How else does one explain all these shenanigans on the Federal bench other than recalling what late Chief MKO Abiola once said: “No one stands all day in the rain for nothing.” The jurist knew in advance that his conduct would be publicly condemned. Yet, he went ahead with the breach of court processes each time. Furthermore, while the Justice, who has acquired notoriety, whether deserved or not, is not the only one on the bench pronouncing hair-raising verdicts concerning election issues – while the National Judicial Council, NJC, headed by the Chief Justice of Nigeria, apparently has done nothing to restrain rampant disregard for established court processes. My colleague, Tony Iredia, summarized the situation last week in his must read column – Nigeria Today: “The other day, a respected retired justice of the Supreme Court asserted that our judiciary now operates like market stalls. Courts of coordinate jurisdiction have continued to give conflicting decisions in breach of warnings by the Chief Justice of the Federation.. In addition to this situation which greatly confuses our people, it has become the norm for parties to a case, to both claim to have won the case.” Iredia has highlighted at least two issues which will render the judiciary a danger to Nigeria in 2027; and why losers might not go to court. First is economic. The market is a transactional institution – unlike what a court of justice should not be. If, as has been asserted, without refutation, Nigerian courts should be classified with Jankara, Monday Market, Utarko, Fegge or Ariara markets, it will serve no purpose for other political parties to go there. Markets sell scarce commodities to the highest bidder. The ruling party can outspend all the other political parties put together; and still have funds left to take the campaign committee to Umrah next year. Going to court will amount to a waste of time and money – which they don’t even have. Second, with the fairness of the judiciary now in question, of what use are the various roles assigned to the Third Estate of the Realm by the Constitution and electoral laws when the verdicts of cases have already been written by the highest bidder? I undertook a short exercise before writing this article. All the reported judgments by courts, in connection with political parties were tabulated. An astonishing 78 per cent went against opposition parties. Are these signs of things to come? INEC: DOUBTFUL PREPAREDNESS AND QUESTIONABLE IMPARTIALITY “Will the elections hold?” – Suleiman A Suleiman, Daily Trust, November 9, 2026. Suleiman asked a question in that article; which should be concerning to every Nigerian. The consequences of the 2027 elections not holding or postponed are too calamitous to be contemplated. Yet, we must learn from a conqueror during the 19th century, Napoleon Bonaparte, 1769-1821, whose instruction to his commanders was: “Bring me the bad news quickly; the good news can wait.” Suleiman has brought us the bad news early in time for us to start thinking about how to manage a potential crisis before it transforms into a national disaster. Nigeria’s unity, always fragile, has never been more severely tested than now – a time when distrust is national and violence prevalent everywhere. Our country is like a room in which inflammable materials are stored – waiting for somebody to inadvertently or deliberately toss fire. Right now, the single most potent match stick in the nation is the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC. To begin with, most people strongly doubt its independence or impartiality. “He who pays the piper dictates the tune” is an adage to which most Nigerians subscribe; and which they readily apply to INEC. The Commission has not done everything to dispel the suspicion of partisanship. Many people were surprised when INEC informed a court that it has no record of the certificates submitted by a presidential contender in 2023 and contesting again in 2027. Was it the truth or pre-meditated obstruction of justice? Either way, it stinks. Suleiman, however, provided evidence which should frighten those who still care about Nigeria’s unity. I am one. One, he pointed out to us that the preliminary register of voters displayed by INEC in October, with promise to publish a final register of voters on December 15, 2026 have raised “a thousand and one legal problems with this release because nearly everything INEC says in this release is not only a direct violation of the Electoral Act 2026, but puts the entire election into a legal peril. By publishing the preliminary voters’ register on October 26, and promising to release the certified copy of the register on December 15, INEC has already breached the law twice.” Let us pause here and consider the implications of what Suleiman has told us. He cited the Sections of the Electoral Act 2026 to support his assertions. The Chairman of INEC, Professor Joash Amupitan, SAN, does not need anybody to interpret the words of an Electoral Act to him. The obvious and troubling questions are: Why is he running INEC like a lawless organization? Is he aware of the repercussions of INEC conducting elections which are in breach of the law? Why is he doing it? Free and fair elections don’t occur by accident. The entire world witnessed three recently – Brazil, Israel and the USA. Brazilians re-elected the incumbent government; Israelis rejected Benjamin Netanyahu and Americans delivered a dirty slap in the face to President Trump. The three elections have one thing in common – an impartial, incorruptible and well-prepared electoral body. Nobody went to court; because the umpire was truly independent. By contrast, INEC is exhibiting all the traits of the Nigerian Factor. Like a crooked referee, certain to award a penalty where none is earned, INEC had made a lot of decisions which negatively impacted opposition parties and not one against the APC; now it might be deliberately obstructing justice. Meanwhile, the voters’ register released has exposed the Commission’s lack of integrity. Only a fool would believe that only the few names detected at first glance to have been cloned have bloated the register. When politicians whose states’ populations are less than 5 million – mostly people under 15 – boast of delivering 4 million votes, INEC should be aware that the votes have been counted in November 2026. More to the point; why is INEC reluctant to release the names of the criminals within its ranks who inflated the register? Are they “our boys” planted as moles to subvert the results if they turn out to be unfavourable? Hungry individuals who steal goats or phones are named and shamed. Those plotting to steal an election and the entire nation are shielded from the public. INEC, except under late Professor Humphery Nwosu, who conducted the June 12, 1993 elections, has developed an unenviable reputation. Amupitan took over from a predecessor who was openly insulted after the 2023 elections. That was bad enough. I don’t condone violence any time, any place or against anybody. But, it is significant that this is the first time the Chairman of INEC would be mobbed long before the elections. What will happen after? · To be continued Follow me on Facebook @ J Israel Biola The post Nigerian politicians preparing for war, not election, by Dele Sobowale appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Being one step ahead of an opportunist
items.description: By Bunmi Sofola SYLVIA admitted that her parents’ marriage and the stoic way her mum yielded her position as the first wife to a much younger and ambitious woman prepared her for the way she handled her relationship with men. Her story: “When a man suddenly discovers he’s scaled the ladder of success faster than he’d envisaged, what does he do when he gets to the top? Chuck his frumpy wife for a more sophisticated model that’s what! And it happened to my mother – a stark illiterate my father too couldn’t read or write, but he was a fairly successful cocoa farmer and although we weren’t exactly rolling in the lap of luxury, we were the envy of our small town – talk about big fish in a small pond indeed! “My dad had been on the war-path with the leadership of the Pentecostal Church we attended. Things finally got to a head, and he broke away to found his own church. A chunk of the congregation from the former church went with him and in a couple of years, his church had ballooned into something he himself never envisaged. As donations kept on pouring in from far and wide, he built a mini estate, installed my mother and her children (four of us) in one of the chalets, then got married to a school certificate holder and made her his main wife. His excuse was that he needed an educated ally to go through the books of the church and welcome visitors in a presentable way. “I don’t want to go through the rage and resentment we from my mother’s side felt as we witnessed this imposter parade herself as an intellectual. My poor father didn’t know that he was the laughing stock of the congregation who sniggered at the clumsy speeches his ‘educated’ wife always made, riddled with mistakes. “I was lucky to have a sharp brain and qualified as a lawyer. But I wasn’t lucky in my choice of a husband. Eventually my marriage hit the rocks after five years and two children. The man I had my third child for wasn’t much better, but I was lucky to meet this influential projects director of a parastatal and my life changed for the better. He took care of all my financial needs and was almost twenty years older than I was. “It is amazing what some women put up with for money. This man was fat and flabby. Whenever he slept over and I watched him asleep with his mouth so wide open I could see his missing teeth and the fillings in some of the rest snoring away without a care in the world. I felt really repulsed. He was definitely not a sight to light the fire in any virile woman’s loins, but he was kind and generous. Let’s face it, he was in his late fifties after all and it must be quite exhausting making love to his wife and God knows who else all the time! “When he was retired and went into politics, I was often with him and through his contacts, I was able to land into the midst of the heavies. I was eventually appointed a special adviser to a top politician – my first class ticket to the gravy train. “I’d reverted to my maiden name by this time and my ex-husband had remarried twice! But now that I was an important government official, I quickly changed back to my married name. He had by now burnt his finger in his business and was always broke, so when I sold him the idea of our coming together because of the kids, he jumped at the chance! His greedy eyes swept over my tastefully furnished quarters as he pretended to give our reunion a thought. He is no fool and his calculating brain must have told him that if he played his cards right, his poverty days were over! “He moved into my official quarters at Abuja and my lover was livid. I re-assured him that my husband was the least of his problems and there was nothing stopping us from carrying on as before. It was an added bonus that he not only knew my husband, Ike, he’d given him a couple of contracts when he was in paid employment, just to shut him up. Not that he suspected anything anyway. “Now my husband is a happy man. He drives new cars, wears designer clothes and shoes – and has his share of female admirers. That never bothers me – live and let live is my motto. Just a couple of months ago, he had to travel to the Far East on one of our projects. When he phoned, Lekan, my ‘benefactor’ was around and actually in bed with me. I told my husband he was around on a visit to Abuja and would be leaving soon, did he want to have a word with him? It gives you a sort of power getting away with a murder like that! My husband had no way of guessing that whenever he was out of town Lekan always sleeps over. I never bother to ask him what he was up to on his frequent jaunts! “I don’t have any idea of what this ‘second chance’ marriage would last, but Ike is the least of my problems. He was a very violent and abusive man when we first got married. Now, with so much affluence around him he’s become a gentleman. I know he’s as calculating as I am and we know we’re both using each other, what we have, really is an open marriage and as long as both of us don’t rock the boat… “Once in a while, I remember my poor mum and hw she suffered the humiliation of being relegated to the background because she didn’t have the financial clout to leave and I feel resentful. Yet, her courage encouraged me to seize happiness whenever I could – using what I have – money, power and position – to get what I want…” Hugh Grant, the famous British international film star was once asked why he was so sure that women were attracted to money. His reply: “Be honest. Suppose you were unattached and some guy you adored were to walk through the door right now. If he could be cloned into one rich guy and one poor guy, who were otherwise exactly the same and were able to choose between the two, which one would you go for?” The same question should be put to men too, don’t you think?! Are Men Really Getting Smaller? These are certainly not the best of times for today’s men. Findings show they’re short, smelly and liars! The case of the shrinking penis! Let’s hope it really is what they do with it and not the size that matters because a recent study shows men’s penises are getting smaller! This shocking discovery by the Life-style Condom Company (with a bit of help from latex-gloved nurses) is bound not to thrill either sexes. Previously, the Kinsey Sex Report put the average penis size at between 6.2 and 6.4 inches, but the condom poll claims it’s now 5.877 inches – with two thirds of the 1,000 men studied measuring between 5.1 and 6.2 inches. This discovery could answer two of our times most perplexing questions: Why vibrator sales are at a record high and why ex-girl-friends keep going back to their well endowed lovers. Short-men Syndrome: It’s official; short men have less luck with the ladies. The discovery, set to shock vertically challenged men everywhere, comes from Southampton Hospital. After studying 3,500 medical records and comparing them to marital status, social class and income, the team claims small babies are programmed to be shy in the womb and small boys, who grow to be short adults, are less likely to marry early. I love you, but … So there’s scientific excuse after all! The reason men have an urge for one-night stand is testosterone. Even though they may believe they have a huge attraction to a woman one night, when reality and or sobriety hits, the feelings disappear as quickly as they arrived. Men are different because the centres for emotion and reason are better connected in a woman’s brain. And, because women aren’t out of control on testosterone, they find it easier to evaluate whether a man is potentially the right partner. Dirty, dirty boys! Despite years of cajoling from the girls and all the cosmetics firms spending hundreds of thousands of Naira to persuade them to use their grooming products, men still spend less than 15 minutes in the bathroom each morning. But, don’t despair! This trend is set to change – a recent Mintel survey found that the under-24 age group are now more likely to spend up to an hour making the effort to look and smell good. items.title: All 16 regional best farmers to receive pick-up vehicles at 2026 Farmers’ Day
items.description: All 16 regional best farmers will receive brand-new pick-up vehicles at this year’s National Farmers’ Day celebration, the Minister of Food and Agriculture, Eric Opoku, has announced. The national best farmer with a disability will also receive a pick-up vehicle and GH¢200,000 at the 42nd edition of the celebration, scheduled for Friday, December 4, 2026, at the University of Energy and Natural Resources (UENR) in Sunyani. Mr Opoku announced the awards during a courtesy call on the Paramount Chief of the Sunyani Traditional Area, Odeefour Ogyeamansan Boahen Korkor II, at the Nana Bosoma Royal Palace in Asufufu, a suburb of Sunyani. The visit was to formally invite the traditional ruler to chair the opening session of the national celebration. The minister described this year’s event as exceptional, noting that it would mark the 42nd anniversary of National Farmers’ Day, which was instituted in 1984. He also disclosed that all former national best farmers since the inception of the awards had been invited to attend the celebration, although four of them had passed away. Odeefour Ogyeamansan Boahen Korkor II welcomed the minister’s visit and pledged the support of the chiefs and people of Sunyani towards the successful organisation of the event.

items.title: State Police: Bravo to Tinubu, but…, by Tonnie Iredia
items.description: One of the most difficult ventures in Nigeria is the amendment of the Constitution of the Federal Republic. The major reason for this is the high threshold set by the constitution in its Section 9 which governs the subject. According to the section, a move to alter a constitutional provision must be supported by at least a two-thirds majority of all members of both Houses of the National Assembly in addition to resolutions approving the alterations by at least 24 of the 36 State Houses of Assembly. A more difficult requirement is set for state creation/boundaries, local government areas or even the amendment procedure itself. In the latter case, a four-fifths majority of federal legislators plus approval from at least 24 State Houses of Assembly is required. But for this threshold, so many new states and local government areas would have for long been created following the unending agitations for such requests. Consequently, several Bills were stalled in the past because of the said constitutional hurdles as well as a number of other factors which include legislative committee bottlenecks, intense political pushback and withheld presidential assent. One of the affected bills was the Social-Media and Online Speech Bills aimed at curbing online falsehood, hate speech, or regulating bloggers and social media platforms. Fierce opposition from civil society, media groups, and other articulate Nigerians had argued that the proposed bills and their subsequent versions could threaten free expression and press freedom. The Electoral Act Amendments especially on electronic transmission of results were similarly controversial attracting public protests and intermittent street demonstrations. Against this backdrop, media reports a few days ago that all the 36 State Houses of Assembly had approved the state police bill must have come to many as an unprecedented achievement by the ruling party and its government. Indeed, nothing else has ever produced what many would call an inexplicable consensus on a volatile divisible subject. The passing of the bill was swift beginning with the Senate which acted on it on June 24, 2026, followed by the House of Representatives which approved it a month later. In less than 4 months, all the 36 state assemblies had approved the bill according to the Clerk to the National Assembly Kamoru Ogunlana thereby exceeding the two-thirds constitutional requirement of at least 24 states. Exactly two days later, Femi Gbajabiamila, the Chief of Staff to the President announced that President Tinubu had received the bill for review with the Attorney-General of the Federation ahead of a formal signing ceremony. On this topic, even the most stringent political opponents of the President have no option than to accept his exceptional mobilization capacity. But then, the way all the relevant institutions and groups have either been lured, persuaded or cowed to follow a common line brings up a fresh fear. One of the reasons this column originally supported the state police issue was the expectation that it would help balance power in the nation. We had hoped that it would reduce the concept of the ‘federal might’ by which the Abuja politicians often overwhelmed state authorities that belonged to different political platforms. It probably never occurred to some Nigerians that there could be a case where all politicians in search of a part of the national cake would generate a ‘consensus ad idem.’ Now that the state police bill has pointed to a direction where the presidency, state governors and every other political grouping could have a common mind, how will balancing be done? It would be recalled that in the past, state governors could not completely crush their political opponents; real or imagined, because the Commissioners of Police in their states declined to obey or were directed to act otherwise making it possible for such opponents to taste some relief. In the new scheme of things who would rescue the oppressed? Although these questions may provoke some fear, they do not evaporate the merits of a state police, they only remind us that there is much to be done before the state police service is operationalized. The much that is to be done that we are harping upon is not the drafting of copious provisions to guide operatives; rather it is more about monitoring leadership. Let us not make the same mistake upon which our constitution was built. For example, although the drafters of our constitution belatedly realized that it is better to ask our media to make government accountable to the people than to leave everything to dispute resolution, Nigeria has no law that sufficiently empowers the media to do the prescribed job. Unlike other countries which appreciate the efficacy of empowering their media, Nigeria expects its media to which it gave an enormous task to derive its power from the general freedom of everyone who got no task. Consequently, our political office holders designed a strategy of doing whatever they wished by ensuring that law enforcement agencies are used to detain any media professional who tries to hold them accountable. No one can stop a governor from using the power bestowed on him by the constitution to set up a police service commission to instead establish a kangaroo body and adorn it with the word ‘independent.’ Can we not perceive how our supposedly independent state electoral commissions count votes of local government elections from bedrooms of state governors? To stop a ruling party from taking over all societal institutions, each of the major political parties can be mandated to nominate one member of the governing council of each institution. In that way it becomes difficult for a governor to use state police against opposition politicians. But if that would politicize our state organs, a second option will be to let nominees to such institutions be made by reputable associations such as the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU) or our Bar or Medical associations as well as apex Labour unions. History should however teach us to exclude unions whose executives are forever visiting state governors to honour them with awards or to seek sponsorship of their annual professional meetings. In setting up a police service commission therefore, it would be wise to avoid a repeat of the type of traps which are usually hidden in our laws or arrangements under the guise of stating rules or laws that would further enhance proper running of institutions. Here, I like to recall a scenario which occurred in 1993 when an interim national government was set up to replace the government of President Ibrahim Babangida who was stepping aside. The enabling law of the regime was a provision that where the government is unwilling or unable to continue, the most senior minister shall take over. This gave room for General Sani Abacha to replace Chief Shonekan. First, why did anyone imagine that Shonekan would not wish to continue? Second, what did the provision mean by the most senior minister? What eyewitnesses like this writer understood was that it was because some soldiers wanted a continuation of military rule that the famous June 12, 1993 elections internationally recognized as Nigeria’s best was annulled. If we relate this experience to the arrangements for state police, this is probably when to seriously ponder over a proposal that says ‘the federalpolice can temporarily intervene in a state during serious breakdowns of public order or rights violations with written presidential authorization and judicial review.’ The proposal does not only encourage people to organize breakdowns that the federal police will intervene in, it also makes the totally erroneous point that the federal police is itself impeccable! A state police service in an emerging nation like Nigeria will have its challenges but because Nigeria runs the federal system of government, state institutions must be allowed to grow and develop to maturity. No room should be given to federal authorities to intervene in state institutions only because the central government appears stronger than the subnational. No matter the shortcomings of state institutions, local officers are better placed to act quickly on incidents and emergencies before they escalate. They also better understand community languages, customs, and terrain, that ably aid intelligence gathering and rural coverage. In addition, state officials are better than federal officials in coordinating security more directly with local residents and traditional institutions. It is indeed an overstatement to argue that if state officials are allowed to do their own functions, the nation will enjoy a healthier growth. It would mean a reduction in federal workload which can ease pressure on federal agencies to have enough room to focus on rising federal crimes and interstate offences. There is therefore no better time than now to thank the current federal government for introducing state policing to Nigeria. Nothing also better underscores the reform than a deliberate arrangement that allows everyone to take control of issues within its jurisdiction. The post State Police: Bravo to Tinubu, but…, by Tonnie Iredia appeared first on Vanguard News .

Le public pourra entendre une combinaison rare pour la scène de concert tunisienne : cinq instruments à vent — la flûte, le hautbois, la clarinette, le basson et le cor. items.title: Terrorists kill Niger village head, five others, abduct residents
items.description: …Governor Bago deploys joint security team to affected community By Clare Nnabuike, Minna Suspected terrorists have killed the village head of Lumma Ba’are community in Borgu Local Government Area of Niger State, Mallam Bawa Muhammad, and five other residents in an attack that also left several people abducted and houses burnt. The attackers reportedly invaded the community at about 5:00 a.m. on Saturday, November 21, 2026, shortly after the Muslim call to prayer, forcing residents to flee into nearby bushes for safety. Sources in the community alleged that the assailants beheaded the village head and burnt his body. They also reported that a newborn baby died after being left inside a house that was set ablaze during the attack. Several residents were reportedly abducted, although the exact number of those taken away had yet to be established. Some residents also alleged that individuals from the community had collaborated with the attackers. However, the claims had not been independently verified as of the time of filing this report. The Niger State Police Command confirmed the attack, saying five people were killed and that joint security teams had been deployed to the area to apprehend the perpetrators. The Police Public Relations Officer, Wasiu Abiodun, said in a statement that the incident was reported at about 5:00 a.m. on November 21. “On 21/11/2026 at about 5am, report received indicated that suspected armed men invaded Lumma Ba’are village, Borgu LGA and attacked the community, while about five persons reportedly lost their lives during the attack. “Joint security teams have been deployed to the location, efforts to apprehend the suspected perpetrators ongoing. Further development will be communicated,” Abiodun stated. Also confirming the incident, the Niger State Commissioner for Information and Orientation, Obed Nuhu Nana, said five other persons sustained injuries and were evacuated to the General Hospital, New-Bussa, where they were receiving medical attention. In a statement, Nana said the attack occurred amid lingering intercommunal tensions in the area, describing the incident as unfortunate and unacceptable. “The Niger State Government condemns the attack on Lumma Ba’are community in Borgu Local Government Area, which claimed the lives of five persons, including the Village Head, Malam Bawa Muhammad. “The attack, according to reports received, occurred at about 5:00 a.m. on Saturday, November 21, 2026, when suspected armed men invaded the community amid lingering intercommunal tensions and launched an assault on residents. “Five other persons sustained injuries and were evacuated to the General Hospital, New-Bussa, where they are currently receiving medical attention. Some houses were also reportedly set ablaze during the incident,” the statement said. The government extended its condolences to the families of the deceased and the entire community, while wishing the injured residents a speedy recovery. Nana said joint security teams had been deployed to the affected community, with efforts being intensified to identify and apprehend those responsible. He assured residents that Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago’s administration was working with relevant security agencies to prevent further attacks and restore peace to the area. The government urged residents to remain calm, avoid taking the law into their hands and provide security agencies with credible information that could assist ongoing investigations. It also reiterated its commitment to protecting lives and property across the state, irrespective of ethnic, religious or communal affiliations. items.title: Customs seize contraband worth N3.52bn in Ogun
items.description: .recover cannabis, codeine syrup, others By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS), Ogun I Area Command, has intercepted and seized contraband goods with a total Duty Paid Value (DPV) of ₦3.52 billion as part of intensified efforts to curb smuggling, protect public health and safeguard the nation’s economy. The seizures, which include 6,037 wraps of cannabis, 20,500 bottles of codeine-containing cough syrup, more than 1.45 million tablets and capsules of various brands, foreign parboiled rice, petroleum products and vehicles, were inspected and paraded by the Comptroller-General of Customs during a visit to the Command. According to a statement issued on Saturday, by the Public Relations Officer of Ogun I Area Command, Assistant Superintendent of Customs Paul Gimba, the total value of the seized items with available valuations stood at **₦3,517,838,700. The statement said the seizures reflected the Command’s sustained efforts to combat smuggling and prevent the circulation of prohibited and potentially harmful products in the country. A breakdown of the intercepted items showed that cannabis accounted for 6,037 wraps, valued at ₦1.268 billion, while 20,500 bottles of cough syrup containing codeine had a Duty Paid Value of ₦147.6 million. The Command also intercepted 828,920 tablets of different brands valued at ₦795.76 million and 627,320 capsules worth ₦376.39 million. Other pharmaceutical products seized included 2,850 ampoules of Enox 4000 injection, valued at ₦17.1 million, and 95 prostate pills worth ₦570,000. The seizures further included 5,173 bags of 50kg foreign parboiled rice, valued at ₦455.22 million, alongside 1,067 used tyres worth ₦52.82 million. In the petroleum products category, Customs intercepted 1,037 kegs of 25 litres of Premium Motor Spirit (PMS), valued at ₦34.22 million, and 1,008 kegs of 25 litres of Automotive Gas Oil (AGO), worth ₦44.35 million. Other seized items comprised 21 packages of walkie-talkies, 185 packages of sanitary pads and diapers valued at ₦18.13 million, 125 live cartridges and two trucks with a combined valuation of ₦144 million. The Command also recorded seizures of several used vehicles, including a 2024 Toyota RAV4 and Toyota Highlander valued at a combined ₦50 million; two Lexus vehicles worth ₦25 million; a 2000 Toyota Hilux valued at ₦11 million; a 2013 Toyota RAV4 worth ₦17 million; and a Toyota Sienna valued at ₦14.7 million. Other vehicles intercepted were a 2010 Toyota Venza valued at ₦14.6 million, an Opel worth ₦7.3 million, a Mazda valued at ₦7.1 million and a 2012 Range Rover Sport worth ₦17.2 million. The Customs Service said the interceptions underscored the Command’s determination to enforce relevant Customs laws, prevent the importation and circulation of prohibited goods and protect Nigeria’s economic interests. It added that the enforcement operations were part of broader efforts to safeguard national security and public health while strengthening the country’s economic resilience. The statement also highlighted the Service’s expanding role in national development, noting that its activities go beyond revenue generation and border enforcement to include community engagement, infrastructure support and trade facilitation. According to the statement, the inspection and parade of the seizures, alongside the commissioning of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) projects, demonstrated the Service’s commitment to combining robust enforcement with initiatives that promote community development. items.title: Rising profile of Tems, Asake and Nigerian artists’ Grammy journey
items.description: By Ayo Onikoyi The voices are getting louder everyday that Asake and Tems are the new King and Queen of Afrobeats respectively. And the Recording Academy confirmed it on November 16, 2026 when it announced the nominees for 2027 Grammy awards. Asake appears just to be coming to his own with two nominations while Tems shatfers the roof with four Grammy nominations in one year. Tems has emerged as Nigeria’s most successful representative in the latest nomination cycle, earning four nominations and further establishing herself as one of the most versatile Nigerian musicians on the international stage. Her recognition in the R&B categories is particularly noteworthy. It demonstrates that her appeal extends beyond the African music market and that her songwriting and vocal abilities are attracting recognition in mainstream American music. The nominations also build on an impressive Grammy history. Tems won her first Grammy in 2023 for her contribution to Future’s “Wait For U”, featuring Drake, which won Best Melodic Rap Performance. She subsequently won Best African Music Performance in 2025 for her reimagining of “Love Me JeJe”. She has also received recognition for her contribution to Beyoncé’s Renaissance, Wizkid’s “Essence” and Rihanna’s “Lift Me Up”, from the Black Panther: Wakanda Forever soundtrack. With two Grammy victories already to her credit, Tems is approaching the 2027 ceremony with an opportunity to increase her collection and further strengthen Nigeria’s presence in international R&B. Asake on the other hand has not won any Grammy – yet. But he appears to be knocking on the door. The “Lonely at the Top” hitmaker has now received four Grammy Award nominations as of November 2026. His nominations are all in the Best African Music Performance category. His flirting with the Recording Academy started in 2024 with his hit “Amapiano” with Olamide, followed by “MMS” with Wizkid in 2025. Once again, he has dragged Wizkid onto the Grammy ballot with their collaboration “Jogodo” and his own solo hit “Gratitude” in 2027 Six Nigerian stars earn 2027 Grammy nominations as Afrobeats expands global reach, with the country securing representation in Best African Music Performance, Best Global Music Album, Best Global Music Performance and Best R&B Song. Joining Tems and Asake on the list are: Burna Boy with one nomination for Dia Dia with Shakira for Best Global Music Performance; Wizkid has one nomination too, for his collaboration with Asake on “Jogodo”; Ayra Starr has two nominations for Best Global Music Album with her hit “Starrgirl” and Best African Music Performance on the “Aye Kan (Are You Coming Back?)” collaboration with Angélique Kidjo and Davido with one nomination as his album “Oriadé” earned a place in the Best Global Music Album category, where it will compete against projects by Tems, Ayra Starr, Anitta and Angélique Kidjo. Nigerian artists Grammy journey Nigerian artists have a rich history with the Recording Academy over the years. But the focus is on the current crop of Afrobeats singers who are making the country proud and leading the charge for Africa’s renaissance. Burna Boy For Burna Boy, the 2027 nomination represents another opportunity to extend a Grammy legacy that has helped establish him as one of Africa’s most recognisable musical exports. His collaboration with Colombian superstar Shakira on “Dai Dai” earned him a place in the Best Global Music Performance category, putting him in contention alongside other international acts. His defining moment came in 2021 when Twice As Tall won Best Global Music Album, making him one of the Nigerian artistes to have secured the prestigious award. He has since received nominations for Love, Damini, I Told Them…, “Last Last”, “City Boys”, “Alone” and “Higher”, among other recordings. The new nomination takes his career tally to 14, according to the Recording Academy’s records, making him Nigeria’s most nominated artiste at the awards. Tems Tems has become the first Nigerian artist to win two Grammy Awards and has demonstrated an ability to compete across African music, global music, hip-hop and R&B categories. Her four nominations in 2027 further underline her growing international recognition. She has received 12 nominations as of November 19, 2026. She is one of Africa’s most successful Grammy-winning female artists. Wizkid Wizkid has won one Grammy Award and received seven nominations as of November 19, 2026. His latest nomination is for the 2027 Grammy Awards. Davido Davido has never won a Grammy Award. As of November 19, 2026, the Nigerian Afrobeats star has received six Grammy nominations across four consecutive editions of the awards, from 2024 to 2027. Davido is among Nigeria’s most repeatedly nominated Afrobeats stars at the Grammys, but he is yet to convert any of his six nominations into a win. Ayra Starr Ayra Starr has never won a Grammy Award. However, she has received four Grammy nominations as of November 19, 2026, including two nominations for the 2027 awards. Asake Asake has four Grammy nominations and zero wins, with two nominations coming at the 69th Grammy Awards in 2027 The post Rising profile of Tems, Asake and Nigerian artists’ Grammy journey appeared first on Vanguard News .
